# Positive hook plethysm at every fixed ideal order

## T-064. An explicit parameterized positive formula

Use T062's parameters
\[
m\ge4,\quad k\ge1,\quad a\ge2k+1,\quad
0\le r\le m-2,\quad t\ge0,\quad\mu\vdash m,
\]
\[
n=a+t-k,\qquad
\lambda=((m-1)a+t-mk-r,a+t,(t+1)^r,t^{m-2-r}),
\tag{FK.1}
\]
and \(\nu=\mu\) for even \(t\), \(\nu=\mu'\) for odd \(t\).
Put \(N=m-1\), \(j=k-1\), and define
\[
D_k=\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}
\left\{\begin{matrix}k-1\\p\end{matrix}\right\}
2^p(p+1)!.
\tag{FK.2}
\]
The braces are the set-partition numbers, with the empty-set
convention. Thus \(D_1=1,D_2=4,D_3=28,D_4=268\).

There is an explicit positive bounded-polytope formula for
\(p_{\mu,(n)}^\lambda\), with at most
\[
1+D_k\bigl(2(m^2+3m-4)-1\bigr)
\tag{FK.3}
\]
pieces, each in at most \(m^2+3m-4\) variables. The construction
below specifies every matrix, selected point and finite tag. Its
running time is bounded by
\[
f(k)(m+k+1)^{\,2k+O(1)}
\operatorname{poly}(\text{binary parameter lengths})
\tag{FK.4}
\]
for an explicitly computable function \(f\), obtained from the finite
loops below. Exact coefficient evaluation and nonvanishing have the
stronger bound \(f(k)\operatorname{poly}(m+\text{input bit length})\).
In particular these are polynomial bounds for every fixed ideal
order \(k\). The ordinary binary-part interpretation applies when
\(t\ge1\), since the output lists \(m\) positive parts. At \(t=0\)
the bound retains an explicit/unary outer-degree parameter.

The exact coefficient identity is
\[
p_{\mu,(n)}^\lambda
=c_{m,a,r}(\nu)-d_{m,k,r}(\nu),
\tag{FK.5}
\]
where the first term is the complete G037 stable-hook coefficient.
Sections 1–2 give a positive bounded-size branching formula for
\(d\), with \(0\le d\le D_k\). Sections 3–4 explicitly remove
exactly \(d\) points from G037's single polytope, proving (FK.3).

### 1. Actual homogenization and monomial-orbit induction

Let \(H=\Lambda^r\mathfrak h_N\). The target of T062's split jet
map is
\[
T_{m,k,r}=
\operatorname{Ind}_{S_N}^{S_m}
\left[
\left(\bigoplus_{h=0}^{j}\operatorname{Sym}^h\mathfrak h_N\right)
\otimes H
\right].
\]
The literal permutation module \(P_N=\mathbb Q^N\) decomposes as
\(\mathbb Q u\oplus\mathfrak h_N\), with
\(u=N^{-1}(1,\ldots,1)\). Multiplication by \(u^{j-h}\) gives the
actual equivariant isomorphism
\[
\bigoplus_{h=0}^{j}\operatorname{Sym}^h\mathfrak h_N
\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Sym}^{j}P_N.
\tag{FK.6}
\]
Its inverse is the homogeneous expansion with respect to this direct
sum. Thus no degree-zero or affine-coordinate character is omitted.

The monomial basis of \(\operatorname{Sym}^jP_N\) has orbits
indexed by partitions \(\rho\vdash j\) with \(p=\ell(\rho)\le N\).
For such an orbit let \(n_0=N-p\), and for each positive integer
\(h\) let \(n_h\) be the number of parts of \(\rho\) equal to \(h\).
Omit zero blocks and write \(B_\rho\) for the number of remaining
blocks. The monomial stabilizer is
\[
K_\rho=S_{n_0}\times\prod_{h\ge1}S_{n_h},
\tag{FK.7}
\]
with a zero-size factor omitted. Sending each coset to its monomial
is an actual permutation-module isomorphism. The tensor-induction
map of HJ.12 therefore gives
\[
T_{m,k,r}\simeq
\bigoplus_{\rho\vdash j,\ \ell(\rho)\le N}
\operatorname{Ind}_{K_\rho}^{S_m}
\operatorname{Res}_{K_\rho}^{S_N}H.
\tag{FK.8}
\]

For a permutation vector, subtract its mean separately on every
nonempty block. This gives the explicit rational decomposition
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{K_\rho}\mathfrak h_N
\simeq
\bigoplus_{b}\mathfrak h_{n_b}\ \oplus\ U_\rho,
\qquad
U_\rho=\{(c_b):\ \sum_b n_bc_b=0\}.
\tag{FK.9}
\]
Here \(U_\rho\) is a trivial module of dimension \(B_\rho-1\).
Taking exterior powers, and using the actual exterior-hook Young
maps already established in G037, gives a sum indexed by
\[
e+\sum_b s_b=r,\qquad
0\le e\le B_\rho-1,\qquad
0\le s_b\le n_b-1.
\tag{FK.10}
\]
The multiplicity is \(\binom{B_\rho-1}{e}\), and the block
representation is the tensor product of hooks
\([(n_b-s_b,1^{s_b})]\). Frobenius induction therefore yields
the entirely positive formula
\[
d_{m,k,r}(\nu)=
\sum_{\rho}\ 
\sum_{\text{(FK.10)}}
\binom{B_\rho-1}{e}
\left[s_\nu\right]\!
\left(
s_{(1)}\prod_b s_{(n_b-s_b,1^{s_b})}
\right).
\tag{FK.11}
\]
The factor \(s_{(1)}\) records the one coordinate fixed by
\(S_N\subset S_m\). Every product coefficient is evaluated by
successive literal Littlewood–Richardson tableaux.

This involves only small skew shapes. When \(n_0>0\), take that
block's hook first; the remaining factors have total size
\(p+1\le k\). When \(n_0=0\), one has \(m=N+1=p+1\le k\),
so the entire computation has at most \(k\) cells. Enumerate only
intermediate diagrams between the starting hook and the requested
\(\nu\), then read each skew tableau right to left, top to bottom,
checking its content, row/column inequalities and prefix lattice
inequalities. These are the exact maps and tableaux of Macdonald
I§9(9.2), p143, whose complete proof pp142–147 was read for this
construction, together with I§7(7.3). No plethysm coefficient or
representation-decomposition oracle enters (FK.11).

### 2. A correction bound independent of the outer degree

The normalized symmetrization map embeds
\(\operatorname{Sym}^jP_N\) into \(P_N^{\otimes j}\).
Tensoring with \(H\) and inducing gives an actual injection of
the target (FK.8) into the corresponding ordered-word module.
Its word orbits are indexed by equality patterns: for \(p\)
distinct coordinate values there are
\(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix}j\\p\end{smallmatrix}\right\}\)
set partitions, each with stabilizer \(S_{N-p}\) fixing the
\(p\) selected coordinates individually.

For \(N-p\ge1\), the same coordinate-mean map gives
\[
\mathfrak h_N\big|_{S_{N-p}}
\simeq\mathfrak h_{N-p}\oplus\mathbb Q^p.
\]
Its \(r\)-th exterior power is a sum of hooks with total multiplicity
at most \(2^p\). Induction to \(S_m\) adds \(p+1\) boxes. For
each starting hook and output, the branching multiplicity is the
number of standard tableaux on that skew shape, at most \((p+1)!\).
When \(N-p=0\), the restricted space has dimension
\(\binom{N-1}{r}\le2^p\); induction from the trivial group has
multiplicity at most \(m!=(p+1)!\). Summing the actual word
orbits proves
\[
0\le d_{m,k,r}(\nu)\le D_k.
\tag{FK.12}
\]
It also proves a useful support fact: every label with \(d>0\)
is obtained from a hook by adding at most \(k\) boxes, or has
total size at most \(k\). Thus each content diagonal contains
at most \(k+1\) cells.

For \(\nu=(m)\), formula (FK.9) gives a sharper fact. A positive
exterior power of a nonzero standard block has no trivial
constituent: its exact hook label is nontrivial. Hence only
\(\Lambda^rU_\rho\) contributes, and
\[
d_{m,k,r}((m))=
\sum_{\rho\vdash k-1,\ \ell(\rho)\le N}
\binom{B_\rho-1}{r}.
\tag{FK.13}
\]
In particular \(d>0\) implies \(r\le k-1\). This also handles
size-one blocks and the orbit with \(j=0\).

### 3. Specified points in the stable-hook polytope

Assume \(d=d_{m,k,r}(\nu)>0\). Choose the parity base
\[
a_0=\begin{cases}2k+1,&a\text{ odd},\\2k+2,&a\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
T062's actual jet surjection at \(a_0\) proves that G037's stable
polytope has at least \(d\) lattice points.

First let \(\nu\ne(m)\). With the notation of HJ.13, its least
numerator degree is
\[
L=b(\nu)+\min_{|S|=r}\sum_{(i,j)\in S}(j-i+1)\ge r+1.
\tag{FK.14}
\]
The inequality is the exact Koszul lowest-degree argument HJ.14.
Each point at degree \(a_0+r\) therefore has total tableau/subset
excess at most \(2k+1\).

Enumerate nonnegative semistandard increments above the row-minimum
filling, of total at most \(2k+1\). Their number is bounded by
\(\binom{m+2k+1}{2k+1}\). Standardize with the proven
left-to-right equal-entry rule and deduplicate. As in T063, this
enumerates every needed standard tableau, because its minimal
semistandard filling has entry sum comajor.

For the retained cell subset, let \(w_0\) be its \(r\)-th smallest
weight. Cells of weight below \(w_0-(2k+1)\) are forced in,
and those above \(w_0+(2k+1)\) are forced out. The middle window
contains at most
\[
(4k+3)(k+1)
\tag{FK.15}
\]
cells by the diagonal bound following (FK.12). Enumerate its
subsets of the required size, discard excess beyond \(2k+1\),
and enumerate the remaining coin partitions, whose degree is
at most \(2k+1\). The empty/full subset endpoints are unique.
Choose the first \(d\) complete valid points in the prescribed
enumeration order. The actual surjection ensures termination.
Increase their weight-two coin coordinate by
\(h=(a-a_0)/2\) to obtain \(d\) distinct points at the requested
degree.

For \(\nu=(m)\), (FK.13) gives \(r\le k-1\), so the parity-base
total degree satisfies \(a_0+r\le3k+1\). Directly enumerate
partitions of that degree into coins \(2,\ldots,\min(m,a_0+r)\).
For each exponent vector \(\beta\), let \(i\) be its least
positive index and enumerate \(r\)-subsets of its other positive
indices. These are exactly G037 HK.19's integer points. Choose
the first \(d\) points.

Their degree transport is explicit even when the least index changes.
Add \(h=(a-a_0)/2\) to \(\beta_2\); when \(h>0\), set the
least-support bit to two, and leave the subset bits unchanged.
The new point satisfies every HK.19 inequality: its subset indices
were larger than the old minimum and hence are larger than two;
their positive exponents remain; the new weight-two exponent is
positive. The map is injective. Subtract the known \(h\) from
\(\beta_2\) to recover the old exponents, recover the old minimum
from those exponents, and keep the unchanged subset. At \(h=0\)
use the identity map. Thus the complete point lists and their
inverses are specified for every outer label.

### 4. Positive cells and precise complexity

Apply the unique-owner deletion procedure HJ.16 to the \(d\)
distinct points. Each step replaces one bounded cell by its
\(2N_{\mathrm{poly}}\) first-difference cells, leaving the others.
The final number is exactly
\(1+d(2N_{\mathrm{poly}}-1)\), bounded by (FK.3).
This gives a literal lattice-set bijection with the stable-hook
polytope minus \(d\) points. The dimension identity is the actual
split jet map T062 and the exact orbit decomposition (FK.8);
these maps establish the requested plethysm coefficient.

For completeness, every complexity assertion follows from the
displayed finite loops. The orbit partition and all nonzero-exponent
blocks in (FK.11) have sizes bounded by \(k\). After their exterior
legs and \(e\) are chosen, the zero-block leg is determined by
\(s_0=r-e-\sum_{b\ne0}s_b\); it is checked against its allowed
range rather than enumerated. Thus the number of exterior choices
depends only on \(k\). Every LR skew shape has
at most \(k\) cells, and its intermediate shapes are selected
from at most \(2^k\) subsets. The target coefficient therefore
takes \(f(k)\operatorname{poly}(m)\) integer operations and has
bit length at most that of \(D_k\). G037 evaluates the stable
term in polynomial bit time in \(m\) and the original degree.
This proves the coefficient/nonvanishing bound.

For the positive matrices, the semistandard increment enumeration
has the stated binomial bound, the subset window has (FK.15)'s
parameter-only size, and the coin degree is bounded by \(2k+1\)
or \(3k+1\). There are at most \(D_k\) deletions. Writing and
checking each full matrix has polynomial cost in its number of
variables and binary parameter lengths. These explicit loops
prove (FK.4), including a computable \(f\), without a hidden
input-dependent precomputation.

The executable fixed_order_hook_positive.py implements exactly these
steps: positive monomial-orbit/exterior/LR correction, bounded-excess
point selection, both degree transports, owner-cell deletion, and
G037's exact coefficient evaluator. It specializes to T061 in the
range \(a\ge3\) and to T063 for \(k=2\). T061's separate valid
\(a=2\) endpoint remains available.

# The closed endpoint for hook jets

## T-065. Every valid parameter with \(a\ge2k\)

For \(m\ge4\), \(k\ge1\), \(t\ge0\), \(\mu\vdash m\), and
\[
0\le r\le\min\{m-2,(m-4)k\},
\]
put
\[
n=k+t,\qquad
\lambda=((m-2)k+t-r,2k+t,(t+1)^r,t^{m-2-r}).
\tag{HE.1}
\]
Let \(\nu=\mu\) for even \(t\), \(\nu=\mu'\) for odd \(t\).
Then T064's positive correction formula remains exact at the endpoint:
\[
p_{\mu,(n)}^\lambda
=c_{m,2k,r}(\nu)-d_{m,k,r}(\nu).
\tag{HE.2}
\]
The correction is the positive monomial-orbit/exterior/LR expression
FK.11. The endpoint has a disjoint positive-polytope formula with
the same bounds FK.2–FK.4. Combined with T064, this covers every
valid hook parameter
\[
a\ge2k,\qquad (m-2)a\ge mk+r
\tag{HE.3}
\]
in FK.1, in varying outer degree, leg and outer label. Exact
evaluation, fixed-order complexity and the encoding qualification
are unchanged.

### 1. The verified scalar regularity input

The primary result used here is Nagel–Trok, *Segre's regularity
bound for fat point schemes*, Ann. Sc. Norm. Super. Pisa Cl. Sci.
(5), XX (2020), 217–237, Theorem5.3 p233. With their notation,
\[
r(X)\le
\max_{\dim L>0}
\left\lceil\frac{w_L(X)-1}{\dim L}\right\rceil.
\tag{HE.4}
\]
Their Lemma3.1(a), p225, identifies \(r(X)\) with the least degree
at which the restriction to the fat point scheme is surjective.
Remark4.3 p228 gives the equivalent floor convention.
Primary publisher PDF:
<https://journals.sns.it/index.php/annaliscienze/article/download/674/660/892>.
The downloaded source and text are nagel_trok_2020.pdf and
nagel_trok_2020.txt in this directory. The complete proof chain
through Theorem5.3 was read, including the matroid partition argument,
the residual-ideal maps and the multiplicity induction; the known
regularity theorem is used with these exact conventions.

Apply it to \(m\) points of multiplicity \(k\) forming the frame
in \(\mathbb P^{m-2}\), with \(m\ge5,k\ge2\). A proper
\(q\)-dimensional linear space contains at most \(q+1\) frame
points: any \(m-1\) representing frame vectors are independent.
Its contribution to (HE.4) is at most
\[
\left\lceil\frac{(q+1)k-1}{q}\right\rceil
=k+\left\lceil\frac{k-1}{q}\right\rceil\le2k-1.
\]
The full-space contribution is also at most \(2k-1\), since
\[
mk-1\le(2k-1)(m-2)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(m-4)k-m+3\ge0,
\tag{HE.5}
\]
and the last quantity is at least \(m-5\) in this range.
Consequently scalar restriction is onto in degree \(2k-1\):
\[
B:\operatorname{Sym}^{2k-1}E^*
\longrightarrow
\bigoplus_{i=1}^m
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(E),[v_i]}/\mathfrak m_i^k.
\tag{HE.6}
\]
The pointwise homogeneous line is trivialized by the same specified
affine vectors \(v_i\) as in T062. Its scalar action on each
stabilizer is trivial. Characteristic-zero scalar extension preserves
the rank of this rational matrix, so the cited bound gives the
surjectivity over \(\mathbb Q\) as well.

### 2. An actual horizontal right inverse

Matrix \(B\) is explicitly the array of Taylor coefficients of
degree-\((2k-1)\) monomials at the frame points on the charts
\(\ell_i=1\). Equip its source and target with rational invariant
positive forms. The proved surjectivity gives the rational
equivariant right inverse
\[
S=B^*(BB^*)^{-1}.
\tag{HE.7}
\]
Thus (HE.6) is an exact algebraic map with a specified splitting,
not an unevaluated rank requirement.

Use T062's degree-one horizontal trivializations
\(H_i(\phi)=\iota_z(\ell_i\wedge\phi)\). Express a desired form
jet at point \(i\) in this basis, apply \(S\) to each scalar jet
supported at \(i\), and multiply the resulting scalar polynomial
by \(H_i(\phi)\). Its coefficient degree is
\((2k-1)+1=2k\), and it is horizontal. At every other point
the scalar jets vanish to order \(k\), so the resulting form jets
do also. Summing over \(i\) gives an actual rational
\(S_m\)-equivariant right inverse for the hook jet map at \(a=2k\).

There are two endpoint cases outside the regularity calculation.
For \(m=4\), validity of (HE.1) forces \(r=0\). The scalar
degree-\(2k\) interpolation HJ.8 already gives the required map,
without a horizontal factor. For \(k=1\), validity gives
\(r\le m-4\), and T061's exact degree-two adjoint/frame splitting
applies. These cover every parameter in (HE.1).

The same ideal-sheaf kernel, flag projection and determinant
comparison as in HJ.2–HJ.3 now give (HE.2). In particular the
jet target, its monomial-orbit action and its Specht correction
are exactly FK.6–FK.11; there is no new parity twist.

### 3. Explicit positive cells at the boundary

At \(a=2k\), the least hook numerator degree is at least \(r+1\).
Thus the tableaux and retained subsets needed in T064's point
selection have total excess at most \(2k-1\), smaller than
the already-proved bound. In the invariant branch, \(d>0\)
implies \(r\le k-1\), and the total degree is at most \(3k-1\).
Run the same finite enumeration directly at the endpoint and
choose the first \(d_{m,k,r}(\nu)\) distinct complete points.
The newly proved surjection ensures that enough points exist.
No parity translation is needed.

Delete those points by the unique-owner first-difference cells.
Their exact count is
\(1+d(2N_{\mathrm{poly}}-1)\), with \(d\le D_k\), proving
the same piece and variable bounds as FK.3. The enumeration has
smaller excess and degree than T064, so its full complexity proof
applies. The file endpoint_hook_positive.py exports all polytope constraint matrices
and supplies both the endpoint evaluator and a route combining
\(a=2k\) with the complete T064 range \(a\ge2k+1\).

The geometric input (HE.4) and the explicit Gram splitting prove
surjectivity; coefficient computation and polytope generation use
only FK.11 and the bounded enumeration. They do not build or
invert the input-sized matrix \(B\) at runtime.

`work/rectangular/HOOK_JET_ENDPOINT_MN_CHECK.tsv`.

Source readings, whole-proof reviews and executed endpoint
comparisons have separate ledger events. The result is a
reformulation and application of the cited regularity theorem
through the explicit hook/flag maps; no novelty claim is made
for the scalar regularity bound.



# The first pair correction for varying hook jets

## T-066. The complete boundary \(a=2k-1\)

Let \(m\ge4\), \(k\ge2\), \(t\ge0\), \(\mu\vdash m\), and
\[
0\le r\le\min\{m-2,(m-4)k-(m-2)\}.
\tag{PB.1}
\]
An upper bound below zero gives an empty parameter range. Put
\[
a=2k-1,\quad n=k-1+t,\quad
\lambda=((m-1)a+t-mk-r,a+t,(t+1)^r,t^{m-2-r}).
\tag{PB.2}
\]
Let \(\nu=\mu\) for even \(t\), and \(\nu=\mu'\) for odd
\(t\). Write \(c_{m,a,r}(\nu)\) for the stable-hook multiplicity
in G037, and \(d_{m,k,r}(\nu)\) for the explicit positive jet
correction FK.11. Define
\[
e_{m,r}(\nu)=
\begin{cases}
0,&r=0,\\
c^{\nu}_{(m-r-1,1^{r-1}),(2)},&r\ge1.
\end{cases}
\tag{PB.3}
\]
The last Littlewood–Richardson coefficient is the horizontal-two-strip
Pieri indicator, hence is zero or one. Then
\[
\boxed{p_{\mu,(n)}^\lambda
=c_{m,2k-1,r}(\nu)-d_{m,k,r}(\nu)+e_{m,r}(\nu).}
\tag{PB.4}
\]
More precisely, \(d_{m,k,r}(\nu)-e_{m,r}(\nu)\) is nonnegative
and at most \(D_k\) of FK.12. Deleting exactly that number of
explicit points from the stable-hook polytope gives a positive
disjoint-polytope formula with at most
\[
1+D_k\bigl(2(m^2+3m-4)-1\bigr)
\tag{PB.5}
\]
pieces, each with at most \(m^2+3m-4\) variables. The matrices
are generated in \(f(k)(m+k)^{2k+O(1)}\) times a polynomial in
the remaining input bit lengths. Exact coefficient evaluation has
the fixed-order bounds of T064. The ordinary binary-input
qualification remains unchanged: a polynomial bound in the stated
encoding requires that \(m\) be explicit/unary or represented by
the \(m\) positive output parts when \(t\ge1\).

Together with T064 and T065, this covers all valid parameters
\(a\ge2k-1\) in their hook family. At \(k=1,a=1\), the
partition inequality would give \(m-2\ge m+r\), so that missing
formal endpoint has no valid input.

### 1. The actual restriction complex and its degree

Set \(E=\mathfrak h_m\), \(R=m-2\), \(F=\mathbf Q^R\),
and
\[
\alpha=(a^{R-r},(a-1)^r),\qquad
N=|\alpha|=(m-2)a-r.
\tag{PB.6}
\]
Condition (PB.1) is exactly \(N\ge mk\), equivalently
\(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\). All entries in (PB.2) are
nonnegative and sum to \(mn\).

Use the specified ideals \(I_i=(\ell_i\otimes F)\) in
\(S=\operatorname{Sym}(E\otimes F)\). G027 FA.4 is an actual
exact complex in degree \(N\), with signed restriction maps and
the orientation of each selected subset. Its kernel is
\((J_k)_N\), where T049 identifies the intersection \(J_k\)
with the literal diagonal quotient of the product of block powers.
Applying the exact \(S_\alpha F\) multiplicity functor preserves
the complex and all \(S_m\) actions. The map back to the balanced
module is FA.6, with the precise factor
\(\operatorname{sgn}^{a+t}\).

For a selected subset of size \(q\), the stabilizer decomposition
FA.13 gives \(W=\mathfrak h_{m-q}\), of dimension
\(d=m-q-1=R-q+1\). The corresponding normal Schur shape
\(\rho\) has size at most \(q(k-1)\), because every selected
normal block is truncated below degree \(k\). Its residual
factor is \(S_{\alpha/\rho}W\).

A semistandard tableau on this skew shape with \(d\) possible
entries has at most \(d\) boxes in each column. This implies
\[
\rho_i\ge\alpha_{i+d}\quad(1\le i\le q-1).
\tag{PB.7}
\]
Indeed, if a column occurs in row \(i+d\) of \(\alpha\) but
not in row \(i\) of \(\rho\), that column of the skew shape
has at least \(d+1\) boxes. Consequently every nonzero residual
factor has
\[
|\rho|\ge(q-1)(a-1)=2(q-1)(k-1).
\tag{PB.8}
\]
For \(q\ge3\), this exceeds \(q(k-1)\), since \(k\ge2\).
Thus every term with at least three selected blocks is zero.
The degree-\(N\) complex therefore has only its ambient,
singleton and pair terms. This is concentration of an already
proved exact complex, rather than a conclusion from an Euler
character alone.

### 2. The ambient and singleton maps

Pad \(\alpha\) by one final zero to length \(\dim E=m-1\).
The perfect exterior-column pairing in the width-\(a\) rectangle
gives the actual map
\[
S_\alpha E\simeq(\det E)^a\otimes
S_{(a,1^r)}E^*.
\tag{PB.9}
\]
The invariant rational form identifies \(E\) with \(E^*\).
Multiplication by the factor \(\operatorname{sgn}^{a+t}\)
from FA.6 changes (PB.9) into precisely the common twist
\(\operatorname{sgn}^t\) of the stable-hook module.

For a singleton, \(W=\mathfrak h_{m-1}\) has dimension \(R\).
Its degree-\(u\) normal factor, \(0\le u<k\), has residual
module \(S_{\alpha/(u)}W\). Complementary exterior pairing
and Pieri give
\[
S_{\alpha/(u)}W\simeq
(\det W)^a\otimes
\bigl(\operatorname{Sym}^uW^*\otimes\Lambda^rW^*\bigr).
\tag{PB.10}
\]
Here every constituent on the right becomes polynomial after the
determinant twist: the largest first part of
\(\operatorname{Sym}^uW^*\otimes\Lambda^rW^*\), before
duality, is at most \(u+1\le k\le a\). More explicitly,
complementing a partition \(\beta\) in the \(a\)-rectangle
identifies a horizontal \(u\)-strip \(\alpha/\beta\) with
a horizontal \(u\)-strip added to \((1^r)\). The ordinary
Pieri rule then proves exactly the multiplicities in (PB.10),
including \(u=0\), \(r=0\), and \(r=R\).

The comparison can be made directly with the original jet map.
On the affine chart at the selected point, FA.8 is the literal
substitution
\(Y_{0a}\mapsto-\sum_jx_jY_{ja}\).
Its degree-\(u\) coefficient map preserves a nonzero least normal
degree, by the invertible generic-matrix argument FA.9. Thus its
associated graded map into the degree-\(u\) form jets is
injective. The complementary Pieri computation (PB.10) proves
equality of those finite dimensions. This is therefore an
isomorphism in each graded piece. The exterior pairing and the
horizontal trivializations HJ.7 give a triangular equivariant
isomorphism on the complete truncated jet spaces; its inverse is
finite triangular elimination. This proves that the singleton
restriction map is the actual hook jet evaluation under these
specified maps.

The determinant in (PB.10) cancels the exponent \(a\) in the
global twist. After removing \(\operatorname{sgn}^t\), the
singleton term is exactly
\[
T_{m,k,r}=\operatorname{Ind}_{S_{m-1}}^{S_m}
\left(\bigoplus_{u=0}^{k-1}\operatorname{Sym}^u
\mathfrak h_{m-1}\otimes\Lambda^r\mathfrak h_{m-1}\right).
\tag{PB.11}
\]
Its multiplicity is the positive formula FK.11 already proved
through actual homogenization, monomial-orbit decomposition,
restricted exterior powers and bounded Littlewood–Richardson
maps.

### 3. The unique pair term and all signs

For a pair, the residual dimension is \(R-1\). If \(r=0\),
condition (PB.7) requires \(\rho_1\ge a=2k-1\), while
the normal total degree is at most \(2k-2\); the term is zero.

For \(r\ge1\), (PB.7) gives \(\rho_1\ge a-1=2k-2\).
Both normal slots must therefore have degree exactly \(k-1\),
and their only surviving shape is \(\rho=(2k-2)\). The
ordinary polynomial multiplication
\[
\operatorname{Sym}^{k-1}F\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{k-1}F
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{2k-2}F
\tag{PB.12}
\]
is its unique Cartan projection. Its inverse on that summand is
the degree-\((k-1,k-1)\) polarization divided by its nonzero
binomial scalar. These are rational maps. Interchanging the two
slots acts trivially on the surviving summand, because (PB.12)
is ordinary commutative multiplication.

The residual Pieri strip must remove the whole bottom row of
\(\alpha\), which has length \(a-1\). That already uses
all normal boxes, so no other row changes. The residual partition
and its actual exterior pairing are
\[
\beta=(a^{R-r},(a-1)^{r-1}),\qquad
S_\beta W\simeq(\det W)^a\otimes\Lambda^{r-1}W^*,
\quad W=\mathfrak h_{m-2}.
\tag{PB.13}
\]
The pair restriction still carries the orientation
\(\operatorname{sgn}_{S_2}\). On its stabilizer
\(S_2\times S_{m-2}\), the factor from FA.6 is
\(\operatorname{sgn}_{S_2}^{a+t}
\operatorname{sgn}_{S_{m-2}}^{a+t}\), while
\((\det W)^a=\operatorname{sgn}_{S_{m-2}}^a\).
Since \(a=2k-1\) is odd, the total exponents on both subgroup
signs are congruent to \(t\). Hence, after the same common
\(\operatorname{sgn}^t\) twist, the pair term is
\[
U_{m,r}=\operatorname{Ind}_{S_2\times S_{m-2}}^{S_m}
\left(\mathbf1\otimes\Lambda^{r-1}\mathfrak h_{m-2}\right)
\quad(r\ge1),\qquad U_{m,0}=0.
\tag{PB.14}
\]
Frobenius induction identifies this with the product of \(h_2\)
and the hook Schur function in (PB.3), proving that indicator.

Every comparison above is equivariant. In particular the
remaining differential is the signed polynomial restriction
\((f_i)\mapsto(f_j|_{ij}-f_i|_{ij})_{i<j}\), composed with
the stated normal Cartan and exterior maps. Its signs are the
ordered-subset signs in FA.4.

### 4. The exact sequence and positive cells

Concentration and the actual comparisons prove the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow\operatorname{sgn}^t\otimes
(S_\lambda\mathbf Q^m)_{(n^m)}
\longrightarrow S_{(a,1^r)}\mathfrak h_m
\longrightarrow T_{m,k,r}
\longrightarrow U_{m,r}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{PB.15}
\]
The left twist equals its own inverse. The last map is onto because
the next term of the exact restriction complex is zero. Thus the
image of the stable-hook jet map is an actual representation whose
\(\nu\)-multiplicity is \(d_{m,k,r}(\nu)-e_{m,r}(\nu)\).
This proves both its nonnegativity and formula (PB.4).

To obtain the positive formula, put
\(c=d_{m,k,r}(\nu)-e_{m,r}(\nu)\). If \(c=0\), retain
the stable-hook polytope. If \(c>0\), the label occurs in the
jet correction. The exact monomial-orbit proof of T064 therefore
gives the same diagonal-width bound \(k+1\); in the row-label
case it gives \(r\le k-1\). The least stable numerator degree
is at least \(r+1\), so the nonrow tableau/subset excess at
\(a=2k-1\) is at most \(2k-2\). In the row case the full
degree is at most \(3k-2\).

Enumerate the low-comajor tableaux, bounded retained-cell subsets
and coin variables exactly as in FK.13–FK.15, with this smaller
budget, and retain the first \(c\) distinct complete points.
For the row label use the same explicit star-basis points.
Sequence (PB.15) proves that the stable coefficient is at least
\(c\), so the exhaustive bounded search supplies all these
points. Each point is checked in the original constraint matrix.
There is no degree translation at this fixed endpoint.

Delete one point at a time from its unique current cell, using
the first coordinate where a lattice point differs, with the
two integral inequalities at that coordinate. All previous
coordinates are fixed to the deleted point. This partitions
the cell minus that point, introduces precisely \(2N_{\rm poly}-1\)
additional pieces, and never changes the underlying bounded
polytope constraints. Induction proves (PB.5), disjointness and
the exact lattice-point count. T064's explicit enumeration and
complexity proof applies with the smaller budget.

The file `pair_boundary_hook_positive.py` exports the literal
polytope matrices, the separate jet and pair multiplicities, and
the direct coefficient evaluator. Its `full_coefficient` and
`full_polytopes` routes combine this boundary with T065 and T064.
The correction uses only FK.11 and a two-cell Pieri test; the
runtime does not construct the restriction-complex matrices.

### 5. Sources and checks

The full actual-complex proof is G027 FA.1–FA.17, strengthened by
the complete diagonal-quotient proof T049 DP.1–DP.10. Those proofs
have been reread for this boundary, including the required

The exterior-column pairing and original hook/flag map are the

Littlewood–Richardson proof used by the finite correction was
read at I§9, pp.142–147. Primary text:
<https://math.berkeley.edu/~corteel/MATH249/macdonald.pdf>.

# Every hook tail at fixed ideal order

## T-067. A complete varying-outer-degree positive formula

Let
\[
m\ge4,\quad k\ge1,\quad a\ge1,\quad t\ge0,
\quad0\le r\le m-2,\quad(m-2)a\ge mk+r,
\quad\mu\vdash m.
\tag{AF.1}
\]
Put
\[
n=a+t-k,\qquad
\lambda=((m-1)a+t-mk-r,a+t,(t+1)^r,t^{m-2-r}),
\tag{AF.2}
\]
and let \(\nu=\mu\) for even \(t\), \(\nu=\mu'\) for odd
\(t\). Condition (AF.1) implies \(a\ge k+1\), so \(n\ge1\),
and is exactly the first-row partition inequality in (AF.2).

There is an explicit positive bounded-polytope formula for every
\(p_{\mu,(n)}^\lambda\) in this entire range. Put
\[
D_k=\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}
\left\{\begin{matrix}k-1\\p\end{matrix}\right\}
2^p(p+1)!.
\tag{AF.3}
\]
The formula has at most
\[
1+D_k\bigl(2(m^2+3m-4)-1\bigr)
\tag{AF.4}
\]
disjoint pieces, each in at most \(m^2+3m-4\) variables.
Every constraint, finite tag and removed point is specified below
and exported by `all_fixed_order_hook_positive.py`.

Exact coefficient evaluation and nonvanishing take
\(f(k)\operatorname{poly}(m+\text{input bit length})\) time.
Generating all positive matrices takes
\[
f(k)(m+k+1)^{2k+O(1)}
\operatorname{poly}(\text{input bit length}).
\tag{AF.5}
\]
Here \(f\) is an explicitly computable function of the ideal
order, supplied by the finite loops in §§3–5. In particular both
are polynomial bounds for every fixed \(k\). For ordinary
binary-part input, the polynomial-size counting interpretation
uses \(t\ge1\), which lists all \(m\) positive output parts,
or an explicit/unary outer-degree parameter. No polynomial-time
assertion in a binary-compressed \(m\), or uniform polynomial
bound in \(k\), is imposed.

The stable range \(n\ge a+t\) is the complete G037 family.
The present statement covers every positive ideal order
\(k=a+t-n\) for the same hook tail. It contains T064–T066,
including every endpoint, by the exact comparisons below.

### 1. The fixed complex and its concentration

Write \(E=\mathfrak h_m\), \(R=m-2\), \(F=\mathbf Q^R\),
and
\[
\alpha=(a^{R-r},(a-1)^r),\qquad
N=|\alpha|=(m-2)a-r\ge mk.
\tag{AF.6}
\]
Use G027's literal frame ideals \(I_i=(\ell_i\otimes F)\)
in \(\operatorname{Sym}(E\otimes F)\), its exact signed
restriction complex FA.4 in degree \(N\), and its actual
balanced-flag map FA.6. Applying the exact \(S_\alpha F\)
multiplicity functor retains every differential and its
\(S_m\)-action. The balanced module is the kernel tensored
by \(\operatorname{sgn}^{a+t}\). T049 gives the actual
diagonal-quotient realization of this kernel, in all degrees.

For a selected subset of size \(q\), the stabilizer is
\(S_q\times S_{m-q}\), and the residual vector space is
\(W=\mathfrak h_{m-q}\), of dimension \(d=m-q-1\).
The normal factor is
\[
T_k(F)^{\otimes q},\qquad
T_k(F)=\bigoplus_{u=0}^{k-1}\operatorname{Sym}^uF.
\tag{AF.7}
\]
Its Schur labels \(\rho\) have at most \(q\) rows and size
at most \(q(k-1)\). The residual factor is
\(S_{\alpha/\rho}W\).

The column argument PB.7 proves that a nonzero residual factor
requires \(\rho_i\ge\alpha_{i+d}\) for \(1\le i\le q-1\).
Consequently
\[
q(k-1)\ge|\rho|\ge(q-1)(a-1),\qquad
q\le Q:=\min\left\{m-2,\left\lfloor\frac{a-1}{a-k}\right\rfloor\right\}
\le k.
\tag{AF.8}
\]
The last inequality follows from \(a\ge k+1\); it also holds
at \(k=1\), when the fraction is one. Thus every term after
the first \(k\) selected-subset terms is zero in the actual
complex. This statement includes the selected-subset orientation;
it is not an unsigned replacement of that complex.

### 2. The exact complementary hook and its two components

Fix the invariant direct sum
\(E=P\oplus W\) of FA.13, where \(P\) has ordered basis
the selected \(\ell_i\)'s and dimension \(q\). Put
\(\beta=(a,1^r)\). The full width-\(a\) exterior-column
pairing is a nondegenerate rational equivariant pairing
\[
S_\alpha E\otimes S_\beta E\longrightarrow(\det E)^a.
\tag{AF.9}
\]
Restrict it to \(GL(P)\times GL(W)\). For a normal partition
\(\rho\subset(a^q)\), padded to length \(q\), the paired
normal partition is
\[
\gamma=(a-\rho_q,\ldots,a-\rho_1).
\tag{AF.10}
\]
This follows from the perfect pairing
\(S_\rho P\otimes S_\gamma P\to(\det P)^a\).
Contract that pairing out of (AF.9). The remaining pairing on
the multiplicity spaces is nondegenerate, since the full pairing
is nondegenerate and distinct normal highest types pair only with
their complementary types. It supplies the actual map
\[
S_{\alpha/\rho}W\simeq
(\det W)^a\otimes S_{\beta/\gamma}W^*.
\tag{AF.11}
\]
The rational normalization is fixed by sending ordered exterior
top wedges to the chosen determinant basis. This construction
commutes with the selected coordinate permutations. Their action
stays entirely in the normal multiplicity space.

Since \(|\rho|\le q(k-1)<qa\), the complement \(\gamma\)
is nonempty. For it to lie in the hook \(\beta\), it must have
the form \((a-A,1^s)\), with
\(0\le s\le\min(q-1,r)\). Its residual skew diagram consists
of one row of length \(A\) and one column of length \(r-s\),
with no common row or column. Row symmetrization and column
antisymmetrization therefore act on disjoint sets of tensor slots.
After ordering the row slots first, their normalized Young maps
give the literal tensor isomorphism
\[
S_{\beta/\gamma}W^*
\simeq\operatorname{Sym}^{A}W^*\otimes\Lambda^{r-s}W^*.
\tag{AF.12}
\]
An empty row or column is the scalar factor. The inverse is the
same slot ordering followed by the normalized symmetric and
exterior projections. No mixed row/column relation remains.

Equations (AF.10)–(AF.12) give exactly the finite list
\[
\rho=\rho(q,s,A):=(a^{q-s-1},(a-1)^s,A),
\tag{AF.13}
\]
where zero parts are omitted, and
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\le s\le\min(q-1,r),\quad r-s\le m-q-1,\\
0\le A\le\min\{a-1,\ q(k-1)-(q-1)a+s\}\le k-q.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AF.14}
\]
A negative upper bound gives an empty list. The leg condition is
exactly the condition that the \(a\)-parts of \(\rho\) fit
inside \(\alpha\), as well as the nonzero exterior-power bound.
The last inequality follows by substituting \(a\ge k+1\) and
\(s\le q-1\). It proves that the entire symmetric decoration
has degree at most \(k-q\). These labels have no repetitions:
\(A\le k-q<a-1\), so their final part cannot merge with an
\((a-1)\)-part.

### 3. Bounded normal representations, with actual maps

Define the genuine \(S_q\)-module
\[
M_{q,k,\rho}=
\operatorname{Hom}_{GL_q}
\left(S_\rho\mathbf Q^q, T_k(\mathbf Q^q)^{\otimes q}\right).
\tag{AF.15}
\]
The first group permutes the \(q\) tensor slots. To specify this
space over \(\mathbf Q\), take monomials in \(q\) blocks of
\(q\) variables, with every block degree below \(k\). Retain
total column weight \(\rho\), and impose the raising equations
\(\sum_i y_{ij}\partial_{y_{i,j+1}}=0\), \(1\le j<q\).
Ordered rational row reduction gives a basis and the actual slot
permutation matrices. This is a finite construction of the
highest multiplicity space, not an unspecified representation
oracle.

Using this space in the original rank \(R\ge q\) changes
nothing. Pad \(\rho\) by zeros. A polynomial of that weight
uses only its first \(q\) column variables; all additional
raising equations vanish, and the previous equations are
unchanged. The inclusion is the actual rank-comparison map and
commutes with every slot permutation.

Write
\(M_{q,k,\rho}=\bigoplus_{\eta\vdash q}
m_{q,k,\rho}^{\eta}[\eta]\). These finitely many nonnegative
integers have the following fully evaluated formula. For a cycle
partition \(\xi\vdash q\), put
\[
P_{q,k,\xi}(X)=\prod_{\ell\in\xi}
\left(\sum_{u=0}^{k-1}h_u(X_1^\ell,\ldots,X_q^\ell)\right),
\quad\delta=(q-1,\ldots,0).
\tag{AF.16}
\]
The cyclic tensor trace, followed by multiplication by the Schur
alternant, gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}(\xi\mid M_{q,k,\rho})=
\sum_{\sigma\in S_q}(-1)^\sigma
[X^{\rho+\delta-\sigma\delta}]P_{q,k,\xi}(X),
\qquad
m_{q,k,\rho}^{\eta}=
\sum_{\xi\vdash q}\frac{\chi^\eta(\xi)}{z_\xi}
\operatorname{tr}(\xi\mid M_{q,k,\rho}).
\tag{AF.17}
\]
The first equality holds because only equal monomials around each
slot cycle contribute to its trace, and the alternating coefficient
selects exactly the dominant Schur label \(\rho\). For completeness,
the small character itself is computed by the same alternating
coefficient applied to
\(\prod_{\ell\in\xi}(X_1^\ell+\cdots+X_q^\ell)\), with
target \(\eta\). This is the explicit Frobenius formula, so
there is no character-table oracle. The second equality is the
finite symmetric-group projector on the already constructed
space (AF.15).

All polynomial degrees here are at most \(q(k-1)\), and
\(q\le k\). Every array, permutation sum and rational kernel
in this step is bounded by a computable function of \(k\) alone.
Even a binary-large \(a\) cannot enlarge a normal calculation:
for \(q\ge2\), a surviving term requires \(a\le2k-1\);
for \(q=1\), its normal label is simply \((A)\), \(A<k\).

### 4. Every stabilizer action and coefficient

The selected-subset orientation is \(\operatorname{sgn}_{S_q}\).
The factor in FA.6 restricts as
\(\operatorname{sgn}_{S_q}^{a+t}
\operatorname{sgn}_{S_{m-q}}^{a+t}\).
Equation (AF.11) contributes
\((\det W)^a=\operatorname{sgn}_{S_{m-q}}^a\).
After removing the common \(\operatorname{sgn}^t\), the
actual \(q\)-th nonambient term is consequently
\[
C_q=\bigoplus_{s,A}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_q\times S_{m-q}}^{S_m}
\left[
\operatorname{sgn}_{S_q}^{a+1}M_{q,k,\rho(q,s,A)}
\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{A}\mathfrak h_{m-q}
\otimes\Lambda^{r-s}\mathfrak h_{m-q}
\right].
\tag{AF.18}
\]
The invariant rational form is the stated map between each
standard module and its dual. The sum is precisely (AF.14).
Thus a small label \(\eta\) in (AF.17) is replaced by
\(\eta'\) when \(a\) is even, and is unchanged when \(a\)
is odd. This accounts for all selected and complementary signs.

The remaining induced multiplicities have a bounded-cell
evaluation. Put \(L=m-q\), \(B=r-s\), and first replace
\(\operatorname{Sym}^{A}\mathfrak h_L\) by its actual split
sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow u\operatorname{Sym}^{A-1}\mathbf Q^L
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{A}\mathbf Q^L
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{A}\mathfrak h_L
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{AF.19}
\]
Here \(u=L^{-1}\mathbf1\), the last map is the symmetric power
of coordinate-mean subtraction, and the direct-sum expansion
\(\mathbf Q^L=\mathbf Q u\oplus\mathfrak h_L\) gives its
equivariant splitting. The first term is zero at \(A=0\).

Let \(c_q(\nu)\) be this explicitly evaluated multiplicity of

=c_{m,a,r}(\nu)-c(m,k,a,r,\nu),\qquad

\tag{AF.20}
\]
Equations (AF.13)–(AF.19) evaluate every signed term in (AF.20)

# Rectangular cases and the normalized Hadamard--Howe period

Run: `/root/rectangular_cases`, 21 November 2026 (Europe/Berlin).
Model: GPT-6 Astra Pro. The inherited effort setting is not exposed to this agent.

This report supplies exact reformulations, proofs, source locators, and finite certificates for the parent paper. The literature results remain attributed to their authors. The labels R-001--R-006 identify findings and explicit dictionaries established in this run; they do not claim priority over the cited classical results.

## Notation

Write

\[
a_\lambda(d[n])=[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{Sym}^d(\operatorname{Sym}^nV)],
\qquad R_{r,s}=(s^r),
\]

with \(\dim V\ge\ell(\lambda)\). Thus \(r\times s\) in the supplied Ikenmeyer--Panova source means \(R_{r,s}\). All decompositions of complex representations below use characteristic zero. The base ring used for normalized integral tensors will be specified separately.

The Hadamard--Howe map is normalized by averaging permutations, so that

\[
h_{d,n}(v_1^n\cdots v_d^n)=(v_1\cdots v_d)^n.
\]

This is the convention of Kumar--Landsberg, §1.2, arXiv:1410.8585v1.

## R-001. A rectangular plethysm coefficient as a one-point lattice count

For every \(r\ge2\), \(n\ge1\),

\[
a_{(n^r)}(r[n])
=\#\{z\in\mathbb Z:2z=n\}
=\begin{cases}1&n\text{ even},\\0&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}
\tag{R-001}
\]

The first equality presents a positive lattice-point formula on the rational zero-dimensional polytope \(\{n/2\}\). The multiplicity-one statement is classical: Howe, *\((\mathrm{GL}_n,\mathrm{GL}_m)\)-duality and symmetric plethysm*, Proposition 4.3, as located explicitly in Kumar--Landsberg §2; also supplied BIP §2(b).

### Proof of the precise lattice-count form

Take \(V=\mathbb C^r\). A tensor in \((\operatorname{Sym}^nV)^{\otimes r}\) is a polynomial on \(r\) covectors, separately of degree \(n\) in each covector. Arrange the covectors as columns of an \(r\times r\) matrix \(X\). On the dense open subset \(\det X\ne0\), an \(\mathrm{SL}_r\)-invariant polynomial depends only on \(\det X\): two invertible matrices with the same determinant differ by left multiplication by an element of \(\mathrm{SL}_r\). Separate homogeneity forces the invariant to be a scalar multiple of \((\det X)^n\). Equality on the dense open subset is equality of polynomials. Thus the invariant space in the ordered tensor product is one-dimensional.

Permutation of the \(r\) covectors acts on this line by \(\operatorname{sgn}^n\). Passing to the outer symmetric power is taking the invariants of this \(S_r\)-action. Since \(r\ge2\), the invariant dimension is one for even \(n\) and zero for odd \(n\). The \(\mathrm{SL}_r\)-invariant summand of homogeneous degree \(rn\) has \(\mathrm{GL}_r\)-highest weight \((n^r)\). Finally, the equation \(2z=n\) has exactly one integral solution for even \(n\) and none for odd \(n\). This proves all displayed equalities.

The same coefficient holds in every \(\dim V\ge r\): Schur-functor multiplicities are stable once the indexed partition fits, by the symmetric-group multiplicity-space realization.

## R-002. The exact square Hadamard--Howe scalar

Fix an even integer \(n\ge2\), let \(V=\mathbb C^n\), and put \(H=S_n\wr S_n\). Index the tensor factors of \(V^{\otimes n^2}\) by the cells \((i,j)\) of an \(n\times n\) array. Let \(e_H\) be the average over permutations within rows and permutations of rows. Let \(\tau\) transpose the array. Then

\[
\operatorname{Sym}^n(\operatorname{Sym}^nV)=e_HV^{\otimes n^2},
\qquad h_{n,n}=e_H\tau e_H.
\]

Define

\[
\delta=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
e_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{\sigma(n)},
\]

put one copy of \(\delta\) in each column, call the resulting tensor \(D\), and put \(I=e_HD\). This \(I\) spans the determinant line from R-001. For a Latin square \(L\), let \(c(L)\) denote the product of its column signs, and let \(E_n-O_n\) be its signed enumeration using the product of all row and column signs. Set

\[
\Delta_n=\sum_{L\text{ Latin}}c(L),\qquad
B_n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{(n+j)!}{j!}.
\]

The normalized scalar is

\[
\boxed{
h_{n,n}(I)=c_n I,\qquad
c_n=\frac{\Delta_n}{(n!)^n}
=\frac{(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(E_n-O_n)}{(n!)^n}
=\frac{B_n}{(n!)^n}\int_{\mathrm{SU}(n)}\prod_{i,j=1}^n u_{ij}\,du.
}
\tag{R-002}
\]

Here Haar measure has total mass one. Kumar--Landsberg Theorem 1.9 proves the associated nonvanishing equivalences; Proposition 2.1 gives the determinant contraction. The present calculation fixes every scalar under the displayed averaging convention. Alpöge, *Square-root cancellation for the signs of Latin squares*, Corollary 5, supplies the last coefficient-to-Haar identity. That paper is separate bibliographic material from the supplied `ALPOGE_remark.pdf`.

### Proof of the scalar

Equip the standard tensor basis with its orthonormal inner product. Let \(t_0\) have entry \(e_i\) in every cell of row \(i\). Although \(t_0\) is invariant under the within-row permutations, it need not be invariant under permutations of rows. The needed pairing still has the value one: every row permutation of \(t_0\) has coefficient \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)^n=1\) in \(D\), so

\[
\langle I,t_0\rangle=\langle D,e_Ht_0\rangle=1.
\tag{R-002a}
\]

Because \(I\) spans the determinant line, write \(h_{n,n}I=c_nI\). Self-adjointness of the averages and the transpose permutation gives

\[
c_n=\langle e_H\tau I,t_0\rangle
=\langle I,\tau e_Ht_0\rangle.
\]

The tensor \(e_Ht_0\) is the average of \(t_0\) over permutations of rows. After applying \(\tau\), those permutations become simultaneous within-row permutations of \(t_1:=\tau t_0\). Since \(I\) is invariant under the within-row permutations,

\[
c_n=\langle I,t_1\rangle=\langle D,e_Ht_1\rangle.
\]

Every row of \(t_1\) is \((e_1,\ldots,e_n)\). Thus \(e_Ht_1\) averages independently over the \(n!\) reorderings in each of its \(n\) rows. A tensor in this average pairs nontrivially with \(D\) exactly when its columns also contain each basis vector once, which is exactly the Latin-square condition. Its coefficient in \(D\) is the product of column signs. Therefore the pairing is \(\Delta_n/(n!)^n\).

### Proof of the parity conversion

This conversion is an identity of total signed sums, not an equality of the two sign functions on each square. Let \(r(L),c(L),s(L)\) be respectively the products of row, column, and symbol-position signs. On the \(n^2\) ordered pairs, define

\[
R:(i,j)\mapsto(i,L_{ij}),\quad
S:(i,s)\mapsto(j,s)\text{ where }L_{ij}=s,
\quad T:(j,s)\mapsto(s,j).
\]

The column permutation \(C:(i,j)\mapsto(L_{ij},j)\) satisfies \(C=TSR\). The transpose permutation \(T\) has sign \(\epsilon=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\), hence \(r(L)c(L)s(L)=\epsilon\). Form the conjugate Latin square \(L'\), with row \(i\), column \(s\), and entry \(j\) specified by \(L_{ij}=s\). Its row-sign product is \(r(L)\), and its column-sign product is \(s(L)\). Its ordinary sign is therefore \(\epsilon c(L)\). The correspondence \(L\mapsto L'\) is a bijection. Summing proves \(\Delta_n=\epsilon(E_n-O_n)\).

### Proof of the Haar normalization

The coefficient \(C_n\) of \(\prod_{i,j}X_{ij}\) in \(\det(X)^n\) is the sum of the products of the signs of the symbol-position permutations in Latin squares. Parastrophy exchanges this with the column-sign sum, so \(C_n=\Delta_n\). Apply Alpöge Corollary 5 to the all-ones multiindex \(\alpha\), with \(k=n\). Its factorial \(\alpha!\) is one, and the displayed factor in that corollary is \(B_n\). Consequently \(\Delta_n=B_n\int\prod u_{ij}\,du\), giving the last equality.

### Exact finite values and a checked bound

The enumeration script `verify_rectangular.py` visits every reduced Latin square for \(n=2,4,6\), with first row and first column fixed. It found:

| \(n\) | Reduced squares | Reduced column-sign sum | All squares | \(\Delta_n\) | \(c_n\) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | -1 | 2 | -2 | \(-1/2\) |
| 4 | 4 | 4 | 576 | 576 | \(1/576\) |
| 6 | 9408 | -2304 | 812851200 | -199065600 | \(-1/699840000\) |

Every reduced square has \(n!(n-1)!\) completions under row and symbol normalization, and the column sign is unchanged for even \(n\). The recursion enumerates all row permutations with their first entry prescribed, rejects exactly repeated column symbols, and at depth \(n\) evaluates the product of column permutation signs. Thus this is a finite exhaustive certificate, not sampling. The certificate asserts only these three orders.

Alpöge Theorem 2, evaluated at \(k=n\), gives the exact inequality

\[
0\le |c_n|^2\le\frac{B_n}{(n!)^{2n}}.
\tag{R-002b}
\]

The value zero belongs to this interval. The unresolved scalar in the square rectangular component is precisely \(\Delta_n\), or equivalently the displayed Haar integral. No lower bound for general even \(n\) is established in this report.

## R-003. A concrete failure of positivity transfer from rectangular Kronecker coefficients

For every \(d,n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le dn-1\),

\[
a_{(dn-k,1^k)}(d[n])=0.
\tag{R-003a}
\]

This vanishing is known: Eugenio Giannelli, *Representations of symmetric groups*, PhD thesis (2015), Theorem 2.1.2, p.38, with proof in §2.3, pp.42--43; Giannelli attributes the earlier Schur-function proof to Langley--Remmel. The short argument below records the exact wreath-product/exterior-power dictionary used in the counterexample. The hook/exterior-power identification is Giannelli Lemma 2.3.3 (also Fulton--Harris, Proposition 3.12 for irreducibility).

In particular,

\[
\boxed{a_{(13,1,1,1)}(4[4])=0,\qquad
g((13,1,1,1),(4^4),(4^4))=1.}
\tag{R-003b}
\]

The parameters in R-003b lie in the stable range of Ikenmeyer--Panova Proposition 2.8: the tail \(\rho=(1,1,1)\) has size three and the inner degree is four. Thus the actual inequality at this point is \(1\ge0\).

### Proof

The finite-group multiplicity formula is

\[
a_\lambda(d[n])=\dim[\lambda]^{S_n\wr S_d}.
\]

For \(N=dn\), the hook Specht module \([N-k,1^k]\) is \(\bigwedge^kU_N\), where \(U_N\) is the standard, sum-zero representation of \(S_N\). Restrict to the base group \(K=S_n^d\). There is an explicit decomposition

\[
U_N=A\oplus U_n^{(1)}\oplus\cdots\oplus U_n^{(d)},
\]

where \(A\) consists of vectors constant within each block and with total sum zero. The base group fixes \(A\) pointwise, and its quotient \(S_d\) acts on \(A\) as \(U_d\). For every \(j=1,\ldots,n-1\), \(\bigwedge^jU_n\) is the nontrivial irreducible hook \([n-j,1^j]\), so it has no \(S_n\)-invariants. The exterior-power decomposition of a direct sum therefore gives

\[
(\bigwedge^kU_N)^K=\bigwedge^kA.
\]

Taking the remaining \(S_d\)-invariants yields zero for every \(k>0\): the exterior powers in their nonzero range are the nontrivial hooks \([d-k,1^k]\), and the remaining exterior powers vanish. The cases \(n=1\) or \(d=1\) are immediate from the same decomposition with zero-dimensional summands. This proves R-003a.

Ikenmeyer--Panova Proposition 6.4 gives

\[
\sum_k g((16-k,1^k),(4^4),(4^4))q^k
=(1+q^3)(1+q^5)(1+q^7).
\]

The coefficient of \(q^3\) is one, proving R-003b. Independently, `verify_rectangular.py` computed the plethysm by the power-sum cycle index \(h_4[h_4]\), paired with the hook character, and the Kronecker coefficient by the Murnaghan--Nakayama character rule followed by the exact conjugacy-class sum. Both computations use rational arithmetic and give the displayed values.

## R-004. The rectangular-hook polytope

For \(1\le r\le s\), \(0\le k\le rs-1\), let

\[
P_{r,k}=\{(x_2,\ldots,x_r)\in[0,1]^{r-1}:
\sum_{i=2}^r(2i-1)x_i=k\}.
\]

Ikenmeyer--Panova Proposition 6.4 gives exactly

\[
g((rs-k,1^k),(s^r),(s^r))=\#(P_{r,k}\cap\mathbb Z^{r-1}).
\tag{R-004}
\]

The proof of this reformulation is the bijection sending a partition into distinct allowed parts \(3,5,\ldots,2r-1\) to its indicator vector. It preserves the sum. R-003 explicitly computes the plethysm coefficient for one of the positive points of this polytope.

## R-005. An explicit vector and multiplicity one for row-extended even rectangles

Take \(k\ge2\), an even integer \(\ell\ge2\), and \(n\ge\ell\). Put

\[
\lambda=(kn-(k-1)\ell,\ell^{k-1}).
\]

Then

\[
a_\lambda(k[n])=1.
\tag{R-005a}
\]

For \(n\ge k\ell\), the same multiplicity in \(\mathbb C[\overline{\mathrm{GL}_{n^2}\det_n}]_k\) is exactly one. This combines the explicit vector below with BIP Propositions 2.3 and 5.6(1), and Theorem 2.5. The equality of multiplicities refines the occurrence statement to the one-dimensional ambient component.

### Proof and normalized nonzero evaluation

Use \(k\) basis vectors and form \(I_{k,\ell}\) by placing the alternating \(k\)-tensor in each of \(\ell\) columns and averaging the within-row and outer permutations. It is a highest weight vector of weight \((\ell^k)\). For nonzero coefficients \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\), direct contraction gives

\[
\big\langle I_{k,\ell},(\sum_{i=1}^k c_iX_i^\ell)^{\otimes k}\big\rangle
=k!\prod_{i=1}^k c_i.
\tag{R-005b}
\]

Indeed, a nonzero determinant contraction assigns distinct basis labels to the \(k\) rows. There are \(k!\) assignments, their signs are raised to the even power \(\ell\), and every assignment has coefficient \(\prod_i c_i\).

Let \(M:\operatorname{Sym}^\ell V\to\operatorname{Sym}^nV\) multiply by \(e_1^{n-\ell}\), and put \(\kappa=\operatorname{Sym}^kM\). The upper triangular unipotent group fixes \(e_1\), so \(\kappa(I_{k,\ell})\) remains a highest weight vector and its weight is \(\lambda\). The map \(M\), and therefore \(\kappa\), is injective. BIP Proposition 5.6(1) says that \(\kappa\) is an isomorphism on these highest weight spaces, since the second part of \((\ell^k)\) equals the initial inner degree \(\ell\). R-001 now gives R-005a.

With normalized symmetric-tensor pairings, the dual map is

\[
M^*=\frac{\ell!}{n!}\partial_{X_1}^{n-\ell}.
\]

For

\[
q=X_1^{n-\ell}\sum_{i=1}^k c_iX_i^\ell
\]

one obtains

\[
M^*q=c_1X_1^\ell+\binom n\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=2}^k c_iX_i^\ell,
\]

and hence

\[
\boxed{\langle\kappa(I_{k,\ell}),q^{\otimes k}\rangle
=k!\binom n\ell^{-(k-1)}\prod_{i=1}^k c_i\ne0.}
\tag{R-005c}
\]

The pairing identity follows directly from the definition of a dual map, also BIP Theorem 5.4. For \(n\ge k\ell\), BIP Theorem 2.5 places every such padded power sum in the determinant orbit closure. Thus the coordinate-ring quotient is nonzero on this one-dimensional highest weight space. Its multiplicity is both at least one and at most the ambient multiplicity one, proving the claimed equality.

## R-006. Scheme, locally free sheaf, and Grothendieck-group dictionary

The following constructions specify the morphisms transporting R-001--R-005.

1. **Group schemes and Schur operations.** The representations are obtained from the standard locally free sheaf of \(\mathrm{GL}_{r,\mathbb Z}\) by tensor, exterior, and symmetric powers. Over \(\mathbb Q\), their identities are identities in \(K_0(\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{GL}_r)\). A principal \(\mathrm{GL}_r\)-bundle on a \(\mathbb Q\)-scheme gives an associated locally free sheaf \(E\). Applying the associated-bundle functor transports each actual natural tensor morphism and each equality in this Grothendieck group to the corresponding sheaf morphism and class in \(K_0(X)\). In particular, the plethystic operation is \([E]\mapsto[\operatorname{Sym}^d(\operatorname{Sym}^nE)]\).

2. **The determinant line and the normalized map.** For R-002, take \(R=\mathbb Z[1/n!]\). The group order \(|H|=(n!)^{n+1}\) is invertible, so all displayed averages are defined over \(R\). Frame change multiplies \(I\) by \(\det(g)^n\). The resulting locally free line is \((\det E)^{\otimes n}\), and the restriction of the natural tensor map to it is multiplication by the exact scalar \(\Delta_n/(n!)^n\). The scalar and the line therefore descend from frames over \(R\) to every locally free \(E\) of rank \(n\). Over the complex fiber, the coordinate multiplicity in the image of this map is the rank of this scalar map.

3. **The Chow scheme and its coordinate map.** The morphism

   \[
   \mu:(E^*)^{\times n}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^n E^*,
   \qquad(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)\longmapsto\ell_1\cdots\ell_n
   \]

   is defined over \(\mathbb Z\). Its pullback on degree-\(d\) coordinate functions lands in separately degree-\(d\) functions, invariant under \(S_n\), and over \(\mathbb Q\) identifies with \(h_{d,n}\). The affine scheme-theoretic image has coordinate algebra \(\operatorname{im}\mu^*\); this realizes the Chow cone and gives \(\ker h_{d,n}=I(\mathrm{Chow}_n)_d\). Thus R-002 is an exact equation for the rank of the rectangular component of a morphism of coordinate algebras. For \(n=2,4,6\), the finite certificates prove rank one in that component. This coordinate-map assertion is also Kumar--Landsberg Lemma 1.5.

4. **The exact \(K_0\) relation.** For a line \(L\) over a field and an endomorphism \(f:L\to L\), its kernel-image-cokernel exact sequence gives \([\ker f]=[\operatorname{coker}f]\). For the map \(f=0\), both classes equal \([L]\); for \(f=1\), both classes are zero. Both endomorphisms have domain and codomain \(L\). This computes exactly the information supplied by the class identity \([L]-[L]=0\). R-002 records the additional morphism \(c_n\operatorname{id}_L\). The associated \(\lambda\)-operation has \(\lambda_t([L])=1+[L]t\), while \(\gamma_t([L]-1)=1+([L]-1)t\); neither formula changes with the chosen endomorphism of the line, as is verified by the two explicit maps.

5. **Finite étale schemes and weights.** Let \(\mathcal L_n^+\) and \(\mathcal L_n^-\) be the constant finite schemes over \(\mathbb Z\) indexed by column-even and column-odd Latin squares. Their virtual class is \([\mathcal L_n^+]-[\mathcal L_n^-]=\Delta_n[\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z]\). Over every finite field, each geometric point contributes one eigenvalue one to \(H_c^0\), and higher cohomology vanishes. Thus the difference of Frobenius traces is exactly \(\Delta_n\). This gives a direct finite-scheme and weight-zero dictionary for the same signed period numerator. For odd \(n>1\), swapping two rows reverses the column sign and gives an involution pairing all squares, so this virtual class and trace are zero. For even \(n=2,4,6\), their values are the three nonzero integers in the certificate. These are exact computations of the maps and classes involved, with no assertion excluding other geometric relations.

The parent paper is to supply the exact SGA/EGA/FGA locators for these standard constructions from its independent archive/SGA audit. This report does not invent unverified exposé or proposition numbers.

All statements in this inventory are attributed results, not new findings. Parameter domains are written explicitly.

\mathcal X=\{(1),(1,1),(1,1,1,1),(1^6),(2,1),(3,1)\}.
\]

## Source-proof audit notes and boundaries of checking

1. IP Theorem 6.1's displayed exception `d^1-2` is a typographical error: Proposition 6.4 and the proof's table use \(d^2-2\). Its additionally stated strict inequality \(g_k>g_{k-2}\) for all \(k\le d^2/2\) also fails literally, for example \(d=7,k=2\) gives \(0>1\). We use the exact Proposition 6.4 instead. This discrepancy is proved by the generating function, rather than silently correcting the printed theorem.

2. In the supplied proof of IP Theorem 4.7, the line \(w<\sqrt{L+7}+1\le(L+1)/2\), with \(w=\max(\lceil\sqrt{L+7}\rceil,7)\), is false at \(L=9\): it asserts \(7<5\). This is a gap in that displayed estimate, not a counterexample to the theorem. The broad theorem is cited as literature, and is not certified here as an independently checked proof. No new proof in this report depends on that estimate. The parent can record this explicitly or omit reliance on Theorem 4.7.

3. The hook counterexample, parity conversion, averaging normalization, and row-extended evaluation were read and checked in full. A first informal scalar derivation had called \(t_0\) invariant under all of \(H\); that statement fails for row permutations. R-002's final proof explicitly averages \(t_0\), uses evenness to compute its pairing, and moves the row permutations through \(\tau\). This repairs the issue without changing the scalar.

4. Computational certificates are exact finite certificates for their stated inputs. They do not certify a universal nonvanishing theorem or the entire supplied literature.

# Canonical-map boundary checks and prime rectangular blocks

Run: /root/rectangular_cases, 21 November 2026 (Europe/Berlin).
Model: GPT-6 Astra Pro. The inherited reasoning-effort setting is not exposed.

This supplements rectangular_report.md. The scalar normalization and the
determinant tensors \(I_{a,b}\) use that report's R-001 and R-002. The new
formulas below are explicit consequences of established results of Glynn,
Drisko, Howe, and the algebra morphism defining the canonical map. No claim
of priority is made for their nonvanishing content. The full surjectivity
bound proved in Sra III remains \(b\ge(a-1)^2\); the results below prove
specified components at smaller degrees.

## Exact map and coefficient conventions

Put \(V=\mathbb C^a\), with its orthonormal basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_a\), and

\[
 R_a=\bigoplus_{b\ge0}\left((\operatorname{Sym}^b V)^{\otimes a}\right)^{S_a}.
\]

The product is componentwise multiplication. Symmetric powers are realized
as invariant tensors by normalized averaging. There is a graded algebra
morphism

\[
 \mu_a:\operatorname{Sym}(\operatorname{Sym}^aV)\longrightarrow R_a,
 \qquad \mu_a(v^a)=v^{\otimes a}.
 \tag{B1}
\]

Its degree-\(b\) component is \(h_{b,a}\). Thus

\[
 h_{b,a}(u_1^a\cdots u_b^a)=(u_1\cdots u_b)^{\otimes a}.
 \tag{B2}
\]

For even \(b\), let \(I_{a,b}\) be obtained by putting the unnormalized
alternating \(a\)-tensor in each of \(b\) columns, and averaging within
the \(a\) rows. Permuting the rows has sign \(\operatorname{sgn}^b=1\),
so further outer averaging makes no change. This tensor satisfies

\[
 \langle I_{a,b},v_1^b\otimes\cdots\otimes v_a^b\rangle
       =\det(v_1,\ldots,v_a)^b.
 \tag{B3}
\]

The inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument. All tensors
appearing in the coefficient calculations have rational real coefficients.
The coefficient at the tensor having row \(i\) constantly \(e_i\) is one.
The determinant line in \(R_{a,b}\) is one-dimensional by R-001. Products
of the determinant tensors satisfy the actual equality in the algebra

\[
 I_{a,b}I_{a,c}=I_{a,b+c}\qquad(b,c\text{ even}).
 \tag{B4}
\]

Indeed, evaluation on arbitrary \(a\) covectors turns both sides into
the product of determinant powers. Such evaluations determine the tensor.

## R-007. Prime-adjacent square scalars and periods

Let \(p\) run through the odd primes, and write

\[
 \mathcal P_n=\int_{\operatorname{SU}(n)}\prod_{i,j=1}^{n}u_{ij}\,du,
 \qquad
 B_n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{(n+j)!}{j!}.
\]

The normalized square scalar from R-002 satisfies

\[
 \boxed{c_{p-1}\in1+p\mathbb Z_{(p)},\qquad
        p^{p-1}c_{p+1}\in1+p\mathbb Z_{(p)}.}
 \tag{R-007a}
\]

In particular these are nonzero scalars, with exact valuations

\[
 v_p(c_{p-1})=0,\qquad v_p(c_{p+1})=1-p,
 \qquad
 v_p(\mathcal P_{p-1})=2-p,\qquad
 v_p(\mathcal P_{p+1})=-p.
 \tag{R-007b}
\]

Here \(\mathbb Z_{(p)}\) denotes the rational numbers whose denominator is
coprime to \(p\); the integral is the rational number identified by the
coefficient formula of R-002.

### Source statements and proof of this normalization

Glynn, *The conjectures of Alon--Tarsi and Rota in dimension prime minus
one*, Theorem 3.2, states

\[
 E_{p-1}-O_{p-1}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]

Drisko, *On the number of even and odd Latin squares of order \(p+1\)*,
Theorem 9, pp. 33--34, states

\[
 E_{p+1}-O_{p+1}\equiv(-1)^{(p+1)/2}p^2\pmod {p^3}.
\]

Both use row-times-column parity. R-002 proves

\[
 \Delta_n=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(E_n-O_n),\qquad
 c_n=\frac{\Delta_n}{(n!)^n},\qquad \mathcal P_n=\frac{\Delta_n}{B_n}.
\]

For even \(n\), \(n(n-1)/2\equiv n/2\pmod2\). Consequently the two
source congruences become

\[
 \Delta_{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
 \qquad \Delta_{p+1}\equiv p^2\pmod {p^3}.
\]

Wilson's theorem gives \((p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p\), and

\[
 \frac{(p+1)!}{p}=(p+1)(p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p.
\]

The exponents \(p-1\) and \(p+1\) are even. Dividing by the corresponding
factorial units proves (R-007a), and its first two valuation assertions.
In \(B_{p-1}\), the numerator factorials from \(p!\) through
\((2p-3)!\) each contain exactly one factor of \(p\), while all denominator
factorials are prime to \(p\). Thus \(v_p(B_{p-1})=p-2\).
In \(B_{p+1}\), the \(p-1\) factorials \((p+1)!,\ldots,(2p-1)!\)
have valuation one, the two factorials \((2p)!\) and \((2p+1)!\)
have valuation two, and the denominator contributes the one factor in
\(p!\). Thus \(v_p(B_{p+1})=(p-1)+4-1=p+2\). This proves the period
valuations. The ranges include \(p=3\).

These calculations use the established prime-adjacent Alon--Tarsi cases;
they do not supply further orders for that conjecture.

## R-008. A canonical determinant block for every prime-minus-one width

For every odd prime \(p\), every \(2\le a\le p-1\), and \(b=p-1\), put

\[
 m_a=e_1\cdots e_a\in\operatorname{Sym}^aV,
 \qquad
 q_{a,b}=\langle I_{a,b},h_{b,a}(m_a^b)\rangle.
\]

Then

\[
 \boxed{q_{a,p-1}\in1+p\mathbb Z_{(p)}.}
 \tag{R-008a}
\]

In particular the canonical map \(h_{p-1,a}\) has rank one on the
target determinant isotypic component \(S_{((p-1)^a)}V\). The tensor
\(m_a^b\) is an explicit test vector for that component.

More explicitly, in tensor degree \(ab\) set

\[
 e_{(b^a)}=\frac{f^{(b^a)}}{(ab)!}
       \sum_{\sigma\in S_{ab}}\chi^{(b^a)}(\sigma)\sigma,
 \qquad N_{a,b}=\langle I_{a,b},I_{a,b}\rangle>0.
\]

This is the central Schur projector, with \(f^{(b^a)}\) the dimension
of the indicated Specht module. Define the concrete source vector

\[
 u_{a,p}=\frac{N_{a,p-1}}{q_{a,p-1}}
             e_{((p-1)^a)}m_a^{p-1}.
 \tag{B5}
\]

It satisfies the exact equality

\[
 h_{p-1,a}(u_{a,p})=I_{a,p-1}.
 \tag{R-008b}
\]

### Proof of the unit contraction

Glynn's Theorem 3.1, together with the formula defining his modular
hyperdeterminant immediately before that theorem, gives the following
coefficient congruence. For an \(a\times a\) matrix \(E=(e_{ij})\)
of nonnegative integers having every row and every column sum \(b=p-1\),

\[
 C_E=[X^E]\det(X)^b
       \equiv\frac{(-1)^a}{\prod_{i,j}e_{ij}!}\pmod p.
 \tag{B6}
\]

Every denominator in (B6) is a unit modulo \(p\). Write a general
degree-\(b\) vector as

\[
 P=\sum_{|\alpha|=b}P_\alpha e^\alpha,
 \qquad
 F(P)=\langle I_{a,b},P^{\otimes a}\rangle.
\]

Let \(M(\alpha)=b!/\prod_j\alpha_j!\). Evaluation of (B3), first on
independent row vectors and then on their monomial expansions, gives
the exact coefficient formula

\[
 F(P)=\sum_E \frac{C_E}{\prod_i M(E_i)}\prod_i P_{E_i},
 \tag{B7}
\]

where \(E_i\) is row \(i\) of \(E\). This accounts for the normalized
embedding of each symmetric monomial. Wilson's theorem gives

\[
 \prod_iM(E_i)\equiv
 \frac{(-1)^a}{\prod_{i,j}e_{ij}!}\pmod p.
\]

Thus every ratio in (B7) is one modulo \(p\). Equivalently, with
\(P(x)=\sum P_\alpha x^\alpha\),

\[
 F(P)\equiv[x_1^b\cdots x_a^b]P(x)^a\pmod p.
 \tag{B8}
\]

Now introduce independent \(z_{ij}\), \(1\le i\le a\), \(1\le j\le b\),
put \(\ell_j=\sum_i z_{ij}e_i\), and substitute
\(P=\ell_1\cdots\ell_b\) in (B8). By (B2), the left side becomes

\[
 \left\langle I_{a,b},h_{b,a}(\ell_1^a\cdots\ell_b^a)\right\rangle.
\]

Its coefficient at the squarefree monomial \(\prod_{i,j}z_{ij}\)
is \((a!)^b q_{a,b}\), since the squarefree coefficient in
\(\ell_j^a\) is \(a!m_a\). On the right side of (B8), the same
coefficient in \(\prod_j\ell_j(x)^a\) is
\((a!)^b(x_1\cdots x_a)^b\), so it becomes \((a!)^b\) after
coefficient extraction in \(x\). The integer \(a!\) is prime to \(p\).
Cancelling it proves (R-008a).

All tensor averages used here have denominators prime to \(p\), because
\(a,b<p\), so the stated congruences are in the specified local ring.

### Proof of the actual preimage

The central projector \(e_{(b^a)}\) commutes with every tensor-position
permutation and every averaging idempotent. In particular it preserves
both nested symmetric powers and commutes with \(h_{b,a}\). On the target
it is orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by \(I_{a,b}\).
Character orthogonality gives this projector formula, and R-001 supplies
the target multiplicity one. Therefore

\[
 h_{b,a}(e_{(b^a)}m_a^b)
   =e_{(b^a)}h_{b,a}(m_a^b)
   =\frac{q_{a,b}}{N_{a,b}}I_{a,b}.
\]

The scalar \(q_{a,b}\) is nonzero by (R-008a). Multiplication by the
factor in (B5) proves (R-008b). Thus the proof identifies the particular
canonical morphism and an explicit source vector.

## R-009. Products and first-row extensions below the full bound

For every odd prime \(p\), \(2\le a\le p-1\), \(t\ge1\), and
\(s\ge0\), set

\[
 b=t(p-1)+s,\qquad
 \lambda=(as+t(p-1),\;\underbrace{t(p-1),\ldots,t(p-1)}_{a-1}).
\]

The following source and image are explicit:

\[
 \boxed{
 h_{b,a}\bigl(u_{a,p}^{\,t}(e_1^a)^s\bigr)
   =I_{a,t(p-1)}(e_1^{\otimes a})^s\ne0.
 }
 \tag{R-009a}
\]

Both sides are highest weight vectors of weight \(\lambda\). Moreover

\[
 [S_\lambda V:\operatorname{im}h_{b,a}]
   =[S_\lambda V:\operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^bV)]=1
 \tag{R-009b}
\]

in every ambient dimension at least \(a\).

### Proof

The image equality follows by applying the algebra morphism (B1), using
(R-008b), (B4), and \(\mu_a(e_1^a)=e_1^{\otimes a}\). Evaluation on
\(a\) covectors gives the nonzero polynomial

\[
 \det(X)^{t(p-1)}\prod_{j=1}^a x_{1j}^{s}.
\]

This proves the asserted nonvanishing without a cancellation assertion.
The determinant vector is highest weight of weight \((t(p-1)^a)\);
the added factor has weight \((as)\) and is killed by the upper triangular
raising operators. The same is true of the source vector (B5), which
lies in a determinant representation over \(\mathbb C^a\). Embedding
\(\mathbb C^a\subseteq V\) gives highest weight vectors in every larger
ambient space, since the additional raising operators differentiate basis
directions absent from these tensors.

For the target multiplicity, set \(\ell=t(p-1)\). The inner-degree
lifting map \(\kappa^a_{\ell,b}\), obtained by multiplying each inner
factor by \(e_1^s\), maps the unique highest weight vector of weight
\((\ell^a)\) to the displayed image. BIP Proposition 5.6(1) applies
because the second part of \((\ell^a)\) is \(\ell\). It identifies the
two highest weight spaces. Howe Proposition 4.3, equivalently R-001,
gives dimension one because \(\ell\) is even. This proves (R-009b).

### Actual boundary families and examples

For each prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), \(p\ge13\), put

\[
 a=(p-1)/2,\qquad t=(a-2)/2,\qquad s=0.
\]

Then \(a\) is even, and (R-009) proves the entire determinant component
at

\[
 b=t(p-1)=a(a-2)=(a-1)^2-1.
 \tag{B9}
\]

Examples are \((a,b)=(6,24),(8,48),(14,168),(18,288),(20,360),
(26,624),(30,840)\). The case \(a=26\) uses \(p=53\) and \(t=12\);
its base rectangle has width \(52\).

Boundary examples in odd outer degree are obtained with \(t=1\) and
positive \(s\). For \((a,b,p)=(7,35,31)\), the image has its unique
component \(S_{(65,30^6)}V\). For \((a,b,p)=(9,63,61)\), the image has
its unique component \(S_{(87,60^8)}V\). The degree sums are respectively
\(65+6\cdot30=7\cdot35\) and \(87+8\cdot60=9\cdot63\).

The square scalar yields a second exact form. For every
\(n\in\{p-1,p+1:p\text{ odd prime}\}\) and \(k\ge1\),

\[
 h_{kn,n}(I_{n,n}^{\,k})=c_n^{\,k}I_{n,kn}\ne0.
 \tag{B10}
\]

This follows directly from R-002 and (B1). For \(n=6,k=4\), the scalar
is \(699840000^{-4}\), since \(c_6=-699840000^{-1}\). This verifies the
determinant component at \((a,b)=(6,24)\) by an explicit rational scalar.

## R-010. What the last common-power step proves at the boundary

Write \(r=a-1\), and consider the actual differential operator

\[
 \Psi_{r,b}=\prod_{i=1}^r(x\cdot\partial_{v_i})^r
\]

on polynomials initially independent of \(x\), separately of degree
\(b\) in each \(v_i\). Sra III Lemma 2.1 and the proof of Theorem 1.3
give its injectivity for \(b\ge r^2\). The supplement's Corollary S8.1
records the quantitative estimate; immediately after it, p. 36, the
author gives the example \(r=5,b=24\).

For every odd \(r\ge3\), put \(b=r^2-1\) and \(V=\mathbb C^r\). Then

\[
 f(v_1,\ldots,v_r)=\det(v_1,\ldots,v_r)^b
 \quad\text{is nonzero and symmetric,}\qquad \Psi_{r,b}f=0.
 \tag{R-010a}
\]

Indeed \(b\) is even, so the determinant power is symmetric. Every term
in the differentiated expression inserts \(r^2=b+1\) copies of the
same vector \(x\) into \(b\) determinant factors. A determinant receiving
two copies of \(x\) vanishes, and every term has such a factor. For even
\(r\), the same determinant polynomial is alternating because \(b\)
is odd. Thus its projection to the symmetric \(r\)-slot input is zero.
This last parity calculation does not classify the other kernel
components.

The arbitrary-common-power full-tensor kernel admits nonrectangular
components. A concrete example of the analogous operator with \(r=3\), power one, and input degree two per slot has an
additional kernel vector on \(V=\mathbb C^2\). Write
\([ij]=x_i y_j-y_i x_j\) and set

\[
 g=[12][13][23].
\]

It has degree two in each vector and transforms by the sign of the slot
permutation. Under \(v_i\mapsto v_i+t_i x\), each bracket is at most
linear in the \(t_i\), and direct expansion gives

\[
 [t_1t_2t_3]\,
 [v_1+t_1x,v_2+t_2x]
 [v_1+t_1x,v_3+t_3x]
 [v_2+t_2x,v_3+t_3x]=0.
 \tag{R-010b}
\]

The two possible terms are
\(-[x,v_2][x,v_3][x,v_1]\) and
\(+[x,v_1][x,v_2][x,v_3]\), which cancel. The vector has
\(\operatorname{GL}_2\)-weight \((3,3)\), whereas the height-three
rectangle of degree two vanishes on \(\mathbb C^2\). This is an exact
counterexample to a uniform rectangular-kernel classification across
arbitrary common powers. It does not
decide the symmetric-input kernel at \(r\) even and power \(r\).

The current proof does not establish full canonical-map surjectivity at
\(b=(a-1)^2-1\) for general odd \(a\). The unconditional improvements in
this report are the specified canonical-map components (R-008--R-009).

## Independent finite coefficient checks

Let \(D_E=[X^E]\operatorname{per}(X)^b\). The coefficient of
\(\prod_{i,j}z_{ij}\) in \(\prod_iP_{E_i}\), after
\(P=\prod_{j=1}^b\ell_j\), is \(D_E\): each of its \(b\) columns
assigns the \(a\) symbols bijectively to the \(a\) tensor rows, and
the resulting row multiplicities are \(E\). Combining this with (B7)
and its \((a!)^b\) squarefree coefficient gives

\[
 q_{a,b}=
 \frac{\sum_E C_ED_E\prod_{i,j}e_{ij}!}
      {(a!)^b(b!)^a}.
 \tag{B11}
\]

The numerator is the Fischer pairing of the determinant power and
permanent power. The program verify_prime_blocks.py computes their
coefficient tables by exact monomial multiplication, checks (B6) at
every exponent matrix, and evaluates (B11). It imports no source-paper
implementation.

| \(a\) | \(b=p-1\) | Exponent matrices checked | Exact \(q_{a,b}\) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 2 | 3 | \(1/4\) |
| 2 | 4 | 5 | \(1/16\) |
| 3 | 4 | 120 | \(1/1296\) |
| 3 | 6 | 406 | \(1/87480\) |
| 4 | 4 | 10147 | \(1/331776\) |
| 3 | 10 | 2211 | \(1/88179840\) |
| 3 | 12 | 4186 | \(281/838061199360\) |

All seven residues are one modulo the indicated prime. The two square
cases also equal \(c_a^2\), using the independently enumerated Latin
scalars in rectangular_report.md. The nondivisible case \((a,b)=(3,4)\)
checks that the general coefficient argument does not require \(a\mid b\).
