\operatorname{Sym}(\operatorname{Sym}^aV^*)
\longrightarrow\mathbb Q[V^a]^{S_a}.
\tag{EP.4}
\]

Its homogeneous degree-\(n\) part lands in separate slot
degree \((n^a)\), identified with
\(\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^nV^*\).
It is exactly the normalized map \(h_{n,a}\): for an
evaluation tensor \(v_1^n\cdots v_a^n\), transpose the
grid, and normalized symmetrization gives
\((v_1\cdots v_a)^n\), with scalar one. This is the same
tensor calculation as (SR.5). In particular, for any two
homogeneous elements \(A,B\),

\[
h_{r+s,a}(AB)=h_{r,a}(A)\,h_{s,a}(B).
\tag{EP.5}
\]

The right multiplication is ordinary multiplication of the
polynomials on \(V^a\). Thus (EP.5) fixes the graded map,
the product, and all normalization factors.

## 2. Every normalized column preimage

For \(1\le j\le a-1\), use \(j+1\) auxiliary slots
\((x_i,y_{i1},\ldots,y_{ij})\), let \(D_{j+1}\) be
their full determinant, and set

\[
P_{a,j}=
\frac{(-1)^j a^{j+1}(a-1)^j}{(j+1)!}
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{j+1}x_i\right)^{a-2}D_{j+1}^{2}
\in\operatorname{Sym}^{j+1}\operatorname{Sym}^aV^*.
\tag{EP.6}
\]

The determinant-square expression is the literal generator
\(F_{j+1,a,j}\) of R-035, with only one maximal minor.
The exact scalar (SR.14), with \(a,n\) exchanged and
\(n=j+1\), gives

\[
\boxed{h_{j+1,a}(P_{a,j})=F_{a,j+1,j}.}
\tag{EP.7}
\]

Indeed the map's scalar is
\((-1)^j(j+1)!/[a^{j+1}(a-1)^j]\), whose reciprocal is
precisely the coefficient in (EP.6). The image is the nonzero
polynomial (SR.4) on the common \(a\) slots.
All determinants in (EP.6) and (EP.7) use the same initial
coordinate flag, so the displayed vectors are highest vectors
with compatible weights.

The top-row padding element is the degree-one polynomial
\(x^a\in\operatorname{Sym}^aV^*\). Its actual image is
\(u=\prod_{i=1}^a x_i\), directly by (EP.3).

## 3. The complete preimage and its highest weight

Let \(j_1,\ldots,j_q\) be the column heights of \(\rho\),
in their usual order. They satisfy

\[
1\le j_l\le a-1,\qquad
\sum_{l=1}^qj_l=d,\qquad
\sum_{l=1}^q(j_l+1)=d+q.
\tag{EP.8}
\]

Form the following actual product in the symmetric algebra
in (EP.4):

\[
\boxed{
P_{a,n,\rho}=(x^a)^{n-d-q}\prod_{l=1}^qP_{a,j_l}.}
\tag{EP.9}
\]

It has degree \(n\); its exponent is nonnegative in the
stated range. Equations (EP.5) and (EP.7) give its exact image

\[
\boxed{
h_{n,a}(P_{a,n,\rho})
=u^{n-d-q}\prod_{l=1}^qF_{a,j_l+1,j_l}.}
\tag{EP.10}
\]

Every factor on the right is a nonzero polynomial on the common
slot space. The coordinate polynomial ring is an integral
domain, so their product is nonzero. Each factor is highest
for the same unipotent subgroup, as is \(u\), so the product
is highest. Its first coordinate weight is
\[
a(n-d-q)+\sum_l\bigl(a(j_l+1)-2j_l\bigr)=an-2d.
\]
Its \(i\)-th tail coordinate is twice the number of columns
of \(\rho\) of height at least \(i\), which is exactly
\(2\rho_i\). Thus its weight is precisely (EP.1), proving
(EP.2) by the explicit preimage (EP.9).

The partition condition also holds throughout the range:
\[
an-2d\ge(a-2)d+aq\ge2q=2\rho_1.
\]
The coordinate construction uses \(\ell(\rho)+1\)
coordinates, so it is nonzero in every dimension at least that
number; Schur functors give the corresponding stable statement.
At \(\rho=\varnothing\), omitted from the main notation,
the actual pure-power preimage \((x^a)^n\) gives the top-row
component for every \(n\ge0\).

For example, putting \(\rho=(2^k,1^j)\) gives the explicit
four-column-tail family

\[
\boxed{
a\ge j+k+1,\quad k\ge1,\quad j\ge0,\quad
n\ge j+2k+2:\quad
\operatorname{mult}_{(an-4k-2j,4^k,2^j)}
\operatorname{im}h_{n,a}\ge1.}
\tag{EP.11}
\]

Its preimage is the product of the two column preimages
\(P_{a,j+k}P_{a,k}\), with the prescribed pure-power padding.
This conclusion retains the possible additional target
multiplicities; (EP.10) specifies the particular nonzero line
that is reached.

## Exact geometric and Grothendieck transport

The image algebra in (EP.4) is the coordinate pullback of the
specified product morphism (EP.3). Its highest vector and
preimage are actual polynomial functions, and (EP.5) is equality
under that pullback. Applying the frame-torsor functor of
SGA6 VI Theorem3.3 to these rational natural tensor maps gives
the associated-bundle maps over a \(\mathbb Q\)-scheme;
the exact projector and weight extraction locators are those
fully specified in R-036 §5. In exact representation \(K_0\),
multiplication is induced by the same tensor and symmetric
multiplication morphisms. The cote133/028 comparison is A012's
explicit tensor-word/Young-coset and Schur-filtered map, with
its rational idempotent splitting. These constructions preserve
the identities (EP.5), (EP.7) and (EP.10) on every local
trivialization and hence globally.


# An exact rank-two fourth-moment canonical block

## R-038. An explicit matrix refinement of the known two-row isomorphism

The whole two-row canonical rank theorem is already G-006 in
`work/root/degree_three_report.md`: Landsberg, *Geometric
Complexity Theory: an introduction for geometers*,
[arXiv:1305.7387v3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1305.7387),
Theorem 7.21, §7.7, printed p.24, states the isomorphism of the
actual map for binary forms. His §7.2, printed pp.19–20,
defines the tensor regrouping, Exercise 7.4 fixes its scalar,
and Proposition 7.6 proves its ideal-kernel description.
Proposition 7.11, printed p.22, identifies the multiplication
pullback with that same normalized map. The additional result
here is the explicit matrix, determinant, inverse, and endpoint
extension line on the particular component below. Its rank
statement specializes the established theorem.

Let \(a,n\ge2\), \(an\ge8\), and \(\dim V\ge2\).
Set \(\lambda=(an-4,4)\). The actual canonical map
\(h_{n,a}:\operatorname{Sym}^n\operatorname{Sym}^aV
\to\operatorname{Sym}^a\operatorname{Sym}^nV\) reaches its
whole target \(\lambda\)-component. Its exact target and
image multiplicities are

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{mult}_{\lambda}\operatorname{im}h_{n,a}
=a_{a,n}^{\lambda}
=\begin{cases}
2,&a,n\ge4,\\
1,&\min(a,n)\le3,\quad\max(a,n)\ge4,\\
0,&a=n=3.
\end{cases}}
\tag{FM.1}
\]

The proof gives the actual two-by-two canonical matrix, its
nonzero determinant, its inverse, and the exact extension line
at inner degree two or three. No comparison of multiplicities
is used in place of the rank calculation, and no historical
novelty claim is made.

## 1. The invariant basis and the exact small-degree extension

For \(a\) lower-coordinate variables \(w_i\), put
\(\bar w=a^{-1}\sum_iw_i\), \(z_i=w_i-\bar w\), and

\[
P_a=\sum_i z_i^4,\qquad
K_a=\left(\sum_i z_i^2\right)^2,\qquad
T_a=a^2-3a+3.
\tag{FM.2}
\]

They are symmetric and translation invariant. The degree-four
invariants of the sum-zero representation \(\mathfrak h_a\)
are spanned by \(P_a,K_a\). To check the spanning claim by
actual polynomials, expand products of power sums according to
the equality partitions of their indices. The discrete equality
partition gives the corresponding monomial-orbit sum with a
nonzero factorial coefficient; all other terms use fewer distinct
indices. This triangular expansion expresses every symmetric
degree-four polynomial in
\(p_4,p_3p_1,p_2^2,p_2p_1^2,p_1^4\).
Restriction to \(p_1=0\) leaves precisely \(p_4,p_2^2\).
The rational Reynolds projector makes restriction onto the
invariant quotient surjective, so this proves the asserted
spanning map on \(\mathfrak h_a\).

For \(a\ge4\), the centered specializations
\((1,-1,0,\ldots)\) and \((1,1,-1,-1,0,\ldots)\)
give pairs \((P_a,K_a)=(2,4)\) and \((4,16)\), whose
determinant is nonzero. Thus the two generators are independent.
For \(a=2,3\), the exact fourth elementary-symmetric identity

\[
24e_4=p_1^4-6p_1^2p_2+3p_2^2+8p_1p_3-6p_4
\tag{FM.3}
\]

has \(e_4=p_1=0\), giving \(K_a=2P_a\). The generator
is nonzero, so the invariant dimension is one.

For slots \((x_i,y_i)\) and \(u=\prod_i x_i\), use
the separate homogenizations

\[
\widehat P_{a,n}=u^nP_a(y_i/x_i),\qquad
\widehat K_{a,n}=u^nK_a(y_i/x_i).
\tag{FM.4}
\]

For \(n\ge4\), these are nonzero polynomials of degree
\(n\) in each slot, and highest coordinate weight
\((an-4,4)\). Their translation invariance is exactly the
raising equation from the first coordinate. T-032 identifies
them with the actual balanced invariant basis: its first
centered column is scaled by \(u\), so a tail degree-four
polynomial acquires \(u^4\); its factor \(u^{n-4}\)
gives (FM.4). This proves the target multiplicities just stated
whenever \(n\ge4\).

We determine the exact polynomial-extension subspace for
\(n=2,3\). The coefficients of \(w_i^4\) in (FM.2) are

\[
[w_i^4]P_a=\frac{(a-1)T_a}{a^3},\qquad
[w_i^4]K_a=\frac{(a-1)^2}{a^2}.
\tag{FM.5}
\]

Thus for \(a\ge4\) their unique nonzero linear combination
with this coefficient zero is

\[
J_a=a(a-1)P_a-T_aK_a.
\tag{FM.6}
\]

It in fact has degree at most two in every variable. For any
symmetric, translation-invariant quartic let \(A\) be its
coefficient of \(w_i^4\), and \(B\) its coefficient of
\(w_i^3w_l\) for \(i\ne l\). The coefficient of
\(w_i^3\) in its zero derivative \(\sum_l\partial_{w_l}\)
is \(4A+(a-1)B\). Hence \(A=0\) forces \(B=0\).
These are exactly all monomials with a variable exponent above
two. Consequently

\[
\widehat J_{a,n}=u^nJ_a(y_i/x_i)
\quad\text{is a nonzero polynomial for all }a\ge4,n\ge2.
\tag{FM.7}
\]

Separate homogenization is polynomial precisely when every
variable exponent of the dehomogenized polynomial is at most
\(n\); its inverse is evaluation at all \(x_i=1\).
This is exactly T-032's extension map in these coordinates.
For \(n=2,3\), (FM.5) therefore forces the line (FM.6),
and the degree bound just proved makes the whole line extend.
Its multiplicity is one. At \(a=3,n=3\), there is only the
single invariant \(P_3\), whose coefficient (FM.5) is
nonzero, so it fails extension and the target multiplicity is
zero. The other pairs with \(a,n\le3\) do not satisfy
\(an\ge8\). This proves every target count in (FM.1),
with its actual polynomial maps.

## 2. Four exact formal sample identities

Use a one-variable formal linear functional with moments
\(1,0,\mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_4\), and apply it independently
in \(a\) variables. Write \(S_l=\sum_i w_i^l\).
Direct expansion gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_a&=S_4-\frac4aS_1S_3+\frac6{a^2}S_1^2S_2
                    -\frac3{a^3}S_1^4,\\
K_a&=S_2^2-\frac2aS_1^2S_2+\frac1{a^2}S_1^4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{FM.8}
\]

Grouping the monomials by their equality patterns gives

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Polynomial}&\text{Independent-slot evaluation}\\ \hline
S_4\text{ or }S_1S_3&a\mu_4\\
S_1^2S_2\text{ or }S_2^2&a\mu_4+a(a-1)\mu_2^2\\
S_1^4&a\mu_4+3a(a-1)\mu_2^2.
\end{array}
\tag{FM.9}
\]

Every term involving a singleton index vanishes because the first
moment is zero. For \(S_1^4\), the three two-pair partitions
give the factor three; for the middle row only its indicated
pair pattern survives. These exhaust all index patterns and
prove the table directly.

Substitution into (FM.8) gives

\[
L^{\otimes a}(P_a)=C_4\mu_4+C_{22}\mu_2^2,\qquad
L^{\otimes a}(K_a)=D_4\mu_4+D_{22}\mu_2^2,
\tag{FM.10}
\]

with the exact coefficients

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_4&=\frac{(a-1)(a^2-3a+3)}{a^2},&
C_{22}&=\frac{3(a-1)(2a-3)}{a^2},\\
D_4&=\frac{(a-1)^2}{a},&
D_{22}&=\frac{(a-1)(a^2-2a+3)}a.
\end{aligned}
\tag{FM.11}
\]

This is a polynomial-functional computation, so it imposes no
positivity assumption on its formal moments.

## 3. The literal two-by-two canonical matrix

Let \(n\ge4\), take linear factors \(\ell_k=(1,v_k)\),
and set \(Q=\prod_k\ell_k\). The normalized tensor pairing
(SR.6) says that the moment of order \(d\le4\) is the
average over ordered distinct indices, divided by
\(n(n-1)\cdots(n-d+1)\). Translation invariance permits
the replacement of all \(v_k\) by their centered values.
For \(\sum_kv_k=0\), put \(P_n=\sum_kv_k^4\),
\(K_n=(\sum_kv_k^2)^2\), and abbreviate

\[
N_2=n(n-1),\qquad N_4=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3).
\]

The exact split-form moments are

\[
\mu_2^2=\frac{K_n}{N_2^2},\qquad
\mu_4=\frac{3K_n-6P_n}{N_4}.
\tag{FM.12}
\]

The second numerator is (FM.3) at \(p_1=0\):
\(24e_4=3p_2^2-6p_4\) is precisely the ordered-distinct
four-index sum. This proves the normalization including the
factor \(4!\).

The exact Chow evaluation (SR.5), followed by (FM.10)–(FM.12),
therefore gives the following matrix for \(h_{a,n}\), with
columns the source basis
\((\widehat P_{a,n},\widehat K_{a,n})\) and rows the
target basis \((\widehat P_{n,a},\widehat K_{n,a})\):

\[
\boxed{
M_{a,n}=\begin{pmatrix}
-6C_4/N_4&-6D_4/N_4\\
3C_4/N_4+C_{22}/N_2^2&3D_4/N_4+D_{22}/N_2^2
\end{pmatrix}.}
\tag{FM.13}
\]

For the basis assertion here take \(a,n\ge4\). The
polynomial identities continue to hold at \(a=2,3\), where
the source generators satisfy \(K_a=2P_a\).
As in R-035, equality on first coordinates one extends by
separate homogeneity to their dense nonzero open set and then
to a polynomial identity everywhere. Thus (FM.13) computes the
specified canonical morphism with its actual normalization.

The complete determinant computation is

\[
C_4D_{22}-D_4C_{22}
=\frac{(a-1)^2(a-2)(a-3)}a,
\tag{FM.14}
\]

because its remaining numerator simplifies as
\[
(a^2-3a+3)(a^2-2a+3)-3(a-1)(2a-3)
=a^2(a-2)(a-3).
\]
Consequently

\[
\boxed{
\det M_{a,n}
=-\frac{6(a-1)^2(a-2)(a-3)}
{a\,n^3(n-1)^3(n-2)(n-3)}\ne0
\qquad(a,n\ge4).}
\tag{FM.15}
\]

Both copies are reached. In particular, to give a preimage for
either target basis vector under \(h_{n,a}\), take its
coordinate column, multiply by
\(M_{n,a}^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(M_{n,a})/\det M_{n,a}\),
and use those two rational coefficients on the source basis
\((\widehat P_{n,a},\widehat K_{n,a})\). Every matrix
entry and scalar in this preimage is explicit in (FM.11)–(FM.15).

## 4. Actual inner-degree-two and inner-degree-three maps

For \(a\ge4\), combine (FM.6) and (FM.10). The
\(\mu_4\) coefficient cancels identically, while the other
coefficient is

\[
a(a-1)C_{22}-T_aD_{22}
=-a(a-1)(a-2)(a-3).
\tag{FM.16}
\]

This follows from the same explicitly factored numerator in
(FM.14). Since \(J_a\) has degree at most two in each
variable, its independent-slot evaluation depends only on the
first two moments. Any arbitrary extension of those moments
to degrees three and four produces the same value; (FM.16)
has no dependence on that extension. It therefore applies
literally to the split form with \(n=2\) or \(n=3\).
The normalized second moment gives the actual identity

\[
\boxed{
h_{a,n}\widehat J_{a,n}
=-\frac{a(a-1)(a-2)(a-3)}{n^2(n-1)^2}
\widehat K_{n,a},
\qquad a\ge4,\quad n=2,3.}
\tag{FM.17}
\]

The target generator is nonzero and the scalar is nonzero.
Each relevant source and target multiplicity is one by §1.
Scalar-one transposition gives the same rank for the map with
\(a,n\) reversed, so all pairs in the second line of
(FM.1) have their asserted rank. The remaining pair \(a=n=3\)
has zero target by the exact extension calculation. This proves
(FM.1) in full, without substituting into the zero denominators
excluded from (FM.12)–(FM.15).

## 5. Scope, transport, and executed checks

All these polynomials are highest vectors for a two-row Schur
functor. The natural Cauchy/Young embeddings put the same
multiplicity spaces into every dimension at least two, and the
canonical map commutes with those embeddings. Thus the computed
matrices give the stated stable Schur multiplicities and the
actual ranks in every declared dimension. The rational frame,
coaction, weight, exact \(K_0\), and cote133/028 morphisms
are precisely those specified with exact SGA/EGA locators in
R-036 §5; applying them to (FM.13) and (FM.17) transports the
actual matrices and their inverse maps to the associated bundles.

The independent script `verify_fourth_moment_block.py` expands
the centered quartics in their literal slot variables, expands
the product linear form, and pairs monomials with exact
multinomial denominators. It checks both generators on two
independent centered specializations for every \(2\le a\le8\),
\(4\le n\le8\), with nonunit first coordinates. It also
checks \(J_a\)'s actual per-variable degree bound and every
\(4\le a\le8,n=2,3\) endpoint on those specializations.
All 160 literal pairings agree with the stated map. The receipt
is `FOURTH_MOMENT_CANONICAL_CHECK.tsv`.

Separately, binary monomial weights count partitions of four and
three inside the \(a\)-by-\(n\) rectangle; their difference
is the two-row multiplicity. The eight partitions involved
are enumerated directly. All 46 valid pairs \(2\le a,n\le8\),
\(an\ge8\) give the target dimensions in (FM.1).
This independent receipt is `FOURTH_MOMENT_BINARY_WEIGHT_CHECK.tsv`.
The ranks are established by the full matrix proof above.


# A higher-row width-four family with an exact canonical scalar

## R-039. The tails \((4,2^{m-2},1)\)

Let \(m\ge2\), \(a\ge m+1\), \(n\ge3\), and
\(\dim V\ge m+1\). Set

\[
\nu=(4,2^{m-2},1),\qquad
\lambda=(an-2m-1,4,2^{m-2},1).
\tag{HO.1}
\]

These are partitions: the first part is at least
\(3(m+1)-2m-1=m+2\ge4\). The exact target and canonical
image multiplicities are

\[
\boxed{
a_{a,n}^{\lambda}=1,\qquad
\operatorname{mult}_{\lambda}\operatorname{im}h_{n,a}
=\begin{cases}
1,&n\ge m+1,\\
0,&3\le n\le m.
\end{cases}}
\tag{HO.2}
\]

The proof gives a polynomial highest vector, an exact scalar
for the actual normalized canonical map, and a rational
preimage in every nonzero case. The family has \(m+1\) rows,
and its second row has size four. The claim makes no historical
novelty assertion.

## 1. An actual invariant-algebra map and the unit bound

Put \(E=\mathbb Q^a\), \(W=\mathfrak h_a\), and let
\(P:E\to W\) be the sum-zero orthogonal projector. For an
auxiliary four-dimensional space \(T\), the following is a
surjective \(GL(T)\)-equivariant graded-algebra morphism:

\[
\operatorname{Sym}(\Lambda^2T\oplus\Lambda^4T)
\otimes\Lambda(\Lambda^3T)
\longrightarrow
\bigl(\Lambda(W\otimes T)\bigr)^{S_a}.
\tag{HO.3}
\]

Its degree-\(d\) generator, \(d=2,3,4\), sends
\(t_1\wedge\cdots\wedge t_d\) to
\(\sum_i(Pe_i\otimes t_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(Pe_i\otimes t_d)\).
The even generators commute and the odd generators
anticommute, so these prescriptions give the displayed
algebra map.

Here is the complete finite-row spanning argument. In
\(\Lambda(E\otimes T)\), label the four Grassmann letters in
each row by \(1,2,3,4\). A row type is a nonempty subset of
these labels. The product of the corresponding row power sums
expands by the equality partition of its occupied row indices.
The discrete equality partition is exactly the injective
row-assignment sum for the chosen types. All other terms
merge at least two row types and use fewer occupied rows;
overlapping types give zero, and disjoint types give their
literal exterior sign. Induction on the number of occupied
rows expresses every injective assignment sum in the power
sums. Every nonzero invariant orbit average is a nonzero
rational multiple of one of these sums. Two equal odd row
types give zero average, since their interchange has sign
minus one; the other stabilizers only give nonzero factorial
factors. This proves spanning including all finite \(a\).
The equivariant projection \(E\to W\) is surjective on
exterior algebras and on invariants, by the equivariant
inclusion \(W\hookrightarrow E\). It kills the singleton
power sums. The remaining generators are precisely (HO.3).

The rational skew-Cauchy Young projectors give the actual
decomposition

\[
\bigl(\Lambda(W\otimes T)\bigr)^{S_a}
=\bigoplus_{\eta_1\le4}
(S_\eta W)^{S_a}\otimes S_{\eta^t}T.
\tag{HO.4}
\]

We determine the multiplicity of
\(\gamma=\nu^t=(m,m-1,1,1)\) in the source of (HO.3).
We use the following explicit description:

\[
\operatorname{Sym}^d(\Lambda^2T)
\simeq
\bigoplus_{q=0}^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}
S_{(d-q,d-q,q,q)}T.
\tag{HO.5}
\]

For completeness, its polynomial maps are obtained as
follows. In the six variables \(X_{ij}\), \(1\le i<j\le4\),
the Pfaffian
\(Q=X_{12}X_{34}-X_{13}X_{24}+X_{14}X_{23}\)
is a \(GL(T)\) determinant vector. Map \(X_{ij}\) to the
\(ij\) minor of a generic two-by-four matrix. The kernel is
\((Q)\): on the chart \(X_{12}\ne0\) the Plücker equation
solves for \(X_{34}\), and every remaining coordinate choice
is realized by a matrix with its first two columns independent.
The quadric \(Q\) is irreducible (its associated bilinear
matrix has rank six), so this chart is dense in the prime
quadric and gives the kernel everywhere.

The degree-\(d\) quotient has the standard two-row tableau
basis for \(S_{(d,d)}T\). To see this in the same coordinates,
order each two-entry minor column increasingly. Among the
two-subsets of \([4]\), the only incomparable pair is
\((1,4),(2,3)\). The replacement
\(X_{14}X_{23}=X_{13}X_{24}-X_{12}X_{34}\) decreases
both offending exponents and introduces neither of them,
so repeated replacement terminates. Comparable
products correspond to semistandard tableaux of shape
\((d,d)\). Their diagonal matrix monomials are distinct,
so these products are independent. The multiplication map
from tensor columns is equivariant and sends the highest
column tensor \((e_1\wedge e_2)^{\otimes d}\) to
\(X_{12}^d\ne0\). Its cyclic highest submodule is a copy
of \(S_{(d,d)}T\), equivalently the image of its rational
Young projector. The semistandard tableau count is the
dimension of this same Schur module. The resulting
nonzero Schur map is therefore an isomorphism onto the
degree-\(d\) quotient.
Consequently multiplication by \(Q\) gives the exact
degree sequence with quotient \(S_{(d,d)}T\).
Complete reducibility splits it; iteration, retaining
the determinant character of each \(Q\), proves (HO.5)
with precisely the displayed multiplicities.

In addition,
\(\Lambda^3T=(\det T)\otimes T^*\), by exterior
contraction. The exterior powers of this four-dimensional
module give, in particular,

\[
\Lambda^1(\Lambda^3T)=\Lambda^3T,\qquad
\Lambda^3(\Lambda^3T)=(\det T)^2\otimes T.
\tag{HO.6}
\]

The total degree \(|\gamma|=2m+1\) is odd. Thus only
exterior degrees one and three can occur in (HO.3).
Exterior degree three has a determinant-square factor,
so all resulting fourth parts are at least two; it
cannot contribute to \(\gamma_4=1\).

For exterior degree one, let \(l\) be the number of
\(\Lambda^4T\) generators. The other factor, by (HO.5),
has shape \((p+l,p+l,q+l,q+l)\), \(p\ge q\ge0\).
Tensoring with \(\Lambda^3T\) adds a vertical three-strip.
This is the actual exterior Pieri map obtained by column
antisymmetrization and the rational Young projector;
each admissible strip has multiplicity one. Since
\(\gamma_4=1\), one has \(l\le1\). At \(l=1\),
subtracting its determinant leaves
\((m-1,m-2,0,0)\); a vertical three-strip cannot lie
in this two-row shape. At \(l=0\), the unique possibility
is

\[
(p,p,q,q)=(m-1,m-1,0,0),\qquad
\text{added rows }1,3,4.
\tag{HO.7}
\]

Indeed the unequal first two parts force the addition in
row one only, and the equal last two parts equal to one
then force their two additions. This gives one copy
also at \(m=2\). Equations (HO.3)–(HO.7) prove

\[
\dim(S_\nu\mathfrak h_a)^{S_a}\le1
\quad\text{for every }a.
\tag{HO.8}
\]

## 2. The centered highest vector and its affine-minor identity

Take \(a\) row vectors \(w_i\in\mathbb Q^m\), and put
\[
\bar w=\frac1a\sum_iw_i,\quad z_i=w_i-\bar w,\quad
S=\sum_i z_i z_i^t,\quad
C_{pqr}=\sum_i(z_i)_p(z_i)_q(z_i)_r.
\]
Define

\[
H_{a,m}=\sum_{i=1}^m C_{11i}\operatorname{adj}(S)_{im}.
\tag{HO.9}
\]

This polynomial is invariant under permutations of the
rows and under common translations. Its complete tensor
\(\sum_iC_{pqi}\operatorname{adj}(S)_{ir}\) transforms
as \((\det\mathbb Q^m)^2\otimes
\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathbb Q^m)\otimes(\mathbb Q^m)^*\).
The formula follows by substituting \(S\mapsto gSg^t\),
\(C\mapsto g^{\otimes3}C\), and the identity
\(\operatorname{adj}(gSg^t)
=(\det g)^2g^{-t}\operatorname{adj}(S)g^{-1}\).
The latter follows for invertible \(S\) by multiplication,
and then for every \(S\) by polynomial continuation.

The component \(p=q=1,r=m\) is killed by all raising
operators \(\sum_i(w_i)_p\partial_{(w_i)_q}\), \(p<q\):
the two covariant indices are already one, and the dual
index is already \(m\). Its diagonal weight is
\((4,2,\ldots,2,1)=\nu\). This is the literal highest
component inside the indicated tensor module.

Let \(R\) and \(B\) be the \(a\)-by-\((m+1)\) matrices
whose \(i\)-th rows are
\[
r_i=(1,(w_i)_1,\ldots,(w_i)_m),\qquad
b_i=(1,(w_i)_1,\ldots,(w_i)_{m-1},(w_i)_1^2).
\]
Then

\[
\boxed{
A_{a,m}:=aH_{a,m}
=\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq[a]\\ |I|=m+1}}
\det R_I\,\det B_I.}
\tag{HO.10}
\]

To prove this equality, apply the determinant-one
translation column operation to \(R\). Apply it to
the linear columns of \(B\), and replace its last
column by \(w_1^2-2\bar w_1w_1+\bar w_1^2=z_1^2\).
This column operation is available because \(m\ge2\)
and \(B\) contains its \(w_1\) column. The determinant
of \(R^tB\) is unchanged. Its first column is now
\((a,0,\ldots,0)^t\); its lower-right block has the
first \(m-1\) columns of \(S\), followed by the column
\((C_{i11})_i\). Expanding first in the first column
and then in the last column gives \(aH_{a,m}\), with
no cofactor sign left over. Cauchy–Binet for
\(R^tB\) gives exactly the right side of (HO.10).

Each row has degree at most one in \(\det R_I\)
and at most two in \(\det B_I\). Thus \(A_{a,m}\)
has degree at most three in every row. It is nonzero
for every \(a\ge m+1\): use centered rows

\[
e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_m,-e_1-\cdots-e_m,
\quad a-m-1\text{ zero rows}.
\tag{HO.11}
\]

Here \(S=I+\mathbf1\mathbf1^t\), so
\(\operatorname{adj}(S)=(m+1)I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^t\),
and \((C_{11i})_i=(0,-1,\ldots,-1)^t\).
The last component of their product is \(-2\).
Therefore \(H_{a,m}=-2\) and \(A_{a,m}=-2a\).

For slots \((x_i,y_i)\), \(u=\prod_i x_i\), define
\[
F_{a,n,m}=u^n A_{a,m}(y_i/x_i).
\tag{HO.12}
\]
This is a polynomial for every \(n\ge3\). More explicitly,
let \(X_I\) have rows \((x_i,y_{i1},\ldots,y_{im})\),
and let \(Y_I\) have rows
\((x_i^2,x_iy_{i1},\ldots,x_iy_{i,m-1},y_{i1}^2)\).
Then

\[
F_{a,n,m}=u^{n-3}\!
\sum_{|I|=m+1}
\left(\prod_{i\notin I}x_i\right)^3
\det X_I\,\det Y_I.
\tag{HO.13}
\]

Every slot has degree exactly \(n\). The two determinant
signs cancel under row permutations. Translation
invariance gives the raising equations from the first
coordinate, and the lower-coordinate calculation gives
all other raising equations. Its highest weight is
therefore the partition \(\lambda\) in (HO.1).
Specializing \(x_i=1\) recovers \(A_{a,m}\), so it
is nonzero.

The exact dehomogenization map evaluates all \(x_i=1\).
Separate homogeneity makes it injective on the fixed
slot degrees. The first-coordinate raising equations
become common-translation invariance, and the remaining
ones give the highest lower weight \(\nu\).
Taking the sum-zero representatives \(z_i=w_i-\bar w\)
is the inverse linear coordinate map on that translation
quotient. The ordinary Cauchy Young projectors on
the polynomial algebra of \(W\otimes\mathbb Q^m\)
identify its highest-\(\nu\) invariant space with
\((S_\nu\mathfrak h_a)^{S_a}\).
This proves the claimed embedding directly; it is the
localized map used in T-032. Its inverse on the present
vector is (HO.12), and (HO.13) proves its finite-degree
extension even when \(n=3<\nu_1\).
Thus (HO.8) and the
nonzero vector prove the target multiplicity one
in (HO.2) for every declared parameter.

## 3. Independent-slot determinant pairing

Let \(L\) be a formal row functional, of total degrees
at most three, with \(L(1)=1\), \(L(w_p)=0\).
Denote its second and third moments by
\(\mu_{pq}=L(w_pw_q)\) and
\(\mu_{pqr}=L(w_pw_qw_r)\).
Apply \(L\) independently to each row of (HO.10).
For each subset \(I\) of size \(m+1\), expanding both
determinants gives
\[
L^{\otimes(m+1)}(\det R_I\det B_I)
=(m+1)!\det M,\qquad M_{pq}=L(r_p b_q).
\tag{HO.14}
\]
Indeed fix the first determinant permutation; changing
the second relative to it gives the determinant of
the pairing matrix, with identical sign. There are
exactly \((m+1)!\) first permutations. This proves
both the matrix and its full factor.

The first column of \(M\) is \((1,0,\ldots,0)^t\).
Its lower-right block is the \(m\)-by-\(m\) matrix
with entries
\[
M'_{pq}=\mu_{pq}\quad(q<m),\qquad
M'_{pm}=\mu_{p11}.
\]
There are \(\binom a{m+1}\) subsets, so

\[
L^{\otimes a}(A_{a,m})
=(a)_{m+1}\det M'.
\tag{HO.15}
\]

Here \((a)_{m+1}=a(a-1)\cdots(a-m)\). This derivation
uses the actual row polynomial and does not require
probability or positivity assumptions on its moments.

## 4. The exact canonical scalar, inverse, and zero endpoints

Take the product \(Q=\prod_{k=1}^n(1,v_k)\), where
\(v_k\in\mathbb Q^m\). The normalized tensor pairing
of SR.5–SR.6 is the independent-slot functional on
(HO.12). Translation invariance permits centering
the \(v_k\). For \(\sum_kv_k=0\), the exact moments are

\[
\mu_{pq}=-\frac{\sum_k(v_k)_p(v_k)_q}{n(n-1)},
\qquad
\mu_{pqr}=
\frac{2\sum_k(v_k)_p(v_k)_q(v_k)_r}{n(n-1)(n-2)}.
\tag{HO.16}
\]

These identities follow by expanding the ordered
distinct-index sums. At order two, the full sum is
zero and removal of the equal-index terms gives the
minus sign. At order three, subtracting the three
pair coincidences and adding the triple coincidence
leaves two copies of the diagonal third sum. The
ordered sums have respectively \(n(n-1)\) and
\(n(n-1)(n-2)\) terms. This argument includes all
repeated coordinate labels in \(\mu_{11i}\).

Factor the first scalar in (HO.16) out of the first
\(m-1\) columns of \(M'\), and the second out of
its last column. The remaining determinant is
\(H_{n,m}=A_{n,m}/n\), by the last-column expansion
already proved. Consequently (HO.15) gives the
actual normalized polynomial identity

\[
\boxed{
h_{a,n}F_{a,n,m}
=c_{a,n,m}F_{n,a,m},\qquad
c_{a,n,m}=
\frac{2(-1)^{m-1}(a)_{m+1}}
{n^{m+1}(n-1)^m(n-2)}.}
\tag{HO.17}
\]

It holds for \(a\ge m+1,n\ge3\), including the zero
target endpoints. Equality at first coordinates one
extends by separate homogeneity to their dense
nonzero open set, and hence everywhere as a
polynomial identity. This proves (HO.17) for the
specified canonical morphism, with no uncomputed
change of bases.

For \(a,n\ge m+1\), both generator lines are nonzero
and the scalar is nonzero. An actual preimage of
\(F_{a,n,m}\) under \(h_{n,a}\) is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{(-1)^{m-1}a^{m+1}(a-1)^m(a-2)}
{2(n)_{m+1}}F_{n,a,m}.}
\tag{HO.18}
\]

For \(3\le n\le m\), the sum defining \(A_{n,m}\)
is empty. More precisely, the source
\(\operatorname{Sym}^n\operatorname{Sym}^aV\)
is a submodule of \((\operatorname{Sym}^aV)^{\otimes n}\).
Successive horizontal-strip Pieri inclusions have
at most \(n\) rows, while \(\lambda\) has \(m+1>n\)
rows. Its source multiplicity is zero. Its target
multiplicity remains one by §2. This proves the
zero-image line of (HO.2), and completes the exact
rank law.

All these constructions use rational tensor, Young,
and determinant maps. The same fixed multiplicity
maps occur in every dimension at least \(m+1\).
Applying the frame-torsor and exact representation
\(K_0\) constructions specified, with primary
SGA/EGA locators, in R-036 §5 transports (HO.17)
and its explicit inverse to the associated bundles.
The coordinate pullback is exactly R-037 EP.3–EP.5,
with its algebra morphism in EP.4;
thus the polynomial functions also give the stated
nonzero Chow coordinate-ring classes.

## 5. Executed finite verification

The script verify_four_one_tail_family.py expands the two
determinants in (HO.13), expands the product linear
form, and pairs every slot monomial with its exact
multinomial denominator. It uses two configurations,
with nonunit first coordinates, for every
\(3\le a,n\le6\), \(2\le m\le\min(a-1,4)\).
One configuration realizes (HO.11), so the stated
nonzero and zero endpoints are both checked. It
also compares the affine-minor sum directly with
the centered Cramer determinant in every case.

The same script independently computes the actual
source and target coefficients by cycle-index
expansion and Murnaghan–Nakayama for every
\(3\le a\le7\), \(3\le n\le5\), \(2\le m\le a-1\).
All 72 literal polynomial pairings and their affine/Cramer
comparisons pass. All 45 target and 45 source coefficients
agree with (HO.2). The receipts are
FOUR_ONE_TAIL_CANONICAL_SCALAR_CHECK.tsv and
FOUR_ONE_TAIL_MN_CHECK.tsv.
The exact scalar and multiplicity proofs above
establish the unbounded families.


# A second higher-row width-four family

## R-040. The tails \((4,3,2^{m-3},1)\)

Let \(m\ge3\), \(a\ge m+2\), \(n\ge3\), and
\(\dim V\ge m+1\). Set
\[
\nu=(4,3,2^{m-3},1),\qquad
\lambda=(an-2m-2,4,3,2^{m-3},1).
\tag{HC.1}
\]
The first part is at least \(m+4\), so this is a partition.
The exact target and canonical-image multiplicities are
\[
\boxed{
a_{a,n}^{\lambda}=1,\qquad
\operatorname{mult}_{\lambda}\operatorname{im}h_{n,a}
=\begin{cases}1,&n\ge m+2,\\0,&3\le n\le m+1.\end{cases}}
\tag{HC.2}
\]
The proof supplies the actual normalized scalar and its inverse.
All parameter ranges here are unconditional; no historical
novelty claim is made.

## 1. The invariant unit bound and the finite exceptional row count

Use R-039's explicit surjection
\[
\operatorname{Sym}(\Lambda^2T\oplus\Lambda^4T)
\otimes\Lambda(\Lambda^3T)
\twoheadrightarrow(\Lambda(\mathfrak h_a\otimes T))^{S_a},
\qquad \dim T=4.
\tag{HC.3}
\]
Its row power-sum generators, signed equality-partition
spanning argument, and the skew-Cauchy Young projectors
are given in HO.3–HO.5. The transpose of the present tail
is \(\gamma=(m,m-1,2,1)\).

Only even exterior degrees of \(\Lambda(\Lambda^3T)\)
can contribute. Exterior degree zero contributes only
paired-row shapes \((p+l,p+l,q+l,q+l)\), by the exact
Pfaffian decomposition HO.5, and therefore misses
\(\gamma\). Exterior degree four is \((\det T)^3\),
so its fourth part is at least three and it also misses
\(\gamma\). The actual exterior contraction map gives
\[
\Lambda^2(\Lambda^3T)=(\det T)\otimes\Lambda^2T.
\tag{HC.4}
\]
Thus exterior degree two reduces to a vertical two-strip
from
\((p+l+1,p+l+1,q+l+1,q+l+1)\).
The final fourth part one forces \(q=l=0\).
The unequal first two parts force \(p=m-2\), with one
box in row one; the other box must be in row three.
This is the unique strip. The exterior Pieri maps
are the column inclusions followed by rational Young
projections, each with multiplicity one. Consequently
\[
\dim(S_\nu\mathfrak h_a)^{S_a}\le1
\quad\text{for every }a.
\tag{HC.5}
\]

One finite row count is needed for the zero endpoint.
When \(a=m+1\), the space \(W=\mathfrak h_a\) has
dimension \(m\). The complementary-column pairing in
the rectangle \((4^m)\) gives the actual isomorphism
\[
S_\nu W=(\det W)^4\otimes
S_{(3,2^{m-3},1,0)}W^*.
\tag{HC.6}
\]
This is induced by the perfect pairings
\(\Lambda^rW\otimes\Lambda^{m-r}W\to\det W\),
one for each of the four columns, followed by the
corresponding Young projectors. The fourth determinant
power is trivial on \(S_a\); the invariant dot product
on \(W\) identifies its dual with \(W\).
The three-column invariant-algebra surjection CT.4
and its explicitly decomposed source CT.5–CT.6 have
only tails \((2^j)\) and \((3,2^j)\). They exclude
\((3,2^{m-3},1)\). Thus the invariant space in (HC.6)
is zero. This proves the exact finite-row vanishing
without deducing it from a vanishing candidate vector.

## 2. The centered tensor and its highest weight

For centered rows \(z_i=w_i-\bar w\in\mathbb Q^m\), put
\[
S=\sum_i z_i z_i^t,\qquad
C_{pqr}=\sum_i(z_i)_p(z_i)_q(z_i)_r.
\]
For invertible \(S\), write \(G=S^{-1}\) and define
\[
A_{ij,kl}=\det(S)(G_{ik}G_{jl}-G_{il}G_{jk}).
\tag{HC.7}
\]
These expressions are the complementary minors of order
\(m-2\), with their alternating cofactor signs.
They therefore define polynomials at every \(S\).
Equivalently this follows by expanding the coefficient
of a two-entry perturbation of \(\det S\).
Set
\[
\mathcal F_{pqr}^{\,s}
=\sum_{i,j,k}C_{pqi}C_{rjk}A_{ij,ks},
\qquad
F_{a,m}=\mathcal F_{112}^{\,m}-\mathcal F_{121}^{\,m}.
\tag{HC.8}
\]

The transformation of (HC.7) under \(S\mapsto gSg^t\)
is \((\det g)^2\) times four contravariant indices.
Contracting it with the two third tensors leaves
three covariant indices and one contravariant index.
The difference in (HC.8) has free covariant labels
\(1,1,2\), and its dual label is \(m\).
The raising operator \(E_{12}\) sends each displayed
summand to \(\mathcal F_{111}^{\,m}\), so it kills
their difference. Every other raising operator kills
both terms: there is no covariant label above two
and the dual label is already \(m\).
Its diagonal weight is
\[
(2,\ldots,2)+2e_1+e_2-e_m
=(4,3,2^{m-3},1)=\nu.
\tag{HC.9}
\]
This proves the exact highest-weight equations.
The tensor is also row-symmetric and translation invariant
by its definition in centered row sums.

## 3. A weighted affine-minor identity and its degree-three cancellation

Let \(R\) have rows
\((1,w_{i1},\ldots,w_{im})\).
Let \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) have rows
\[
(1,w_{i1},\ldots,w_{i,m-1},w_{i1}^2),
\qquad
(1,w_{i1},\ldots,w_{i,m-1},w_{i1}w_{i2}),
\]
respectively. The assumption \(m\ge3\) ensures that
both linear columns \(w_1,w_2\) occur in each \(B\).
For \(|I|=m+1\), define
\[
L_{I,p}=(a-m-1)\sum_{i\in I}w_{ip}
-(m+1)\sum_{i\notin I}w_{ip}.
\]
The polynomial
\[
\boxed{
D_{a,m}:=-a^2F_{a,m}
=\sum_{|I|=m+1}\det R_I
\bigl(L_{I,2}\det(B_1)_I-L_{I,1}\det(B_2)_I\bigr)}
\tag{HC.10}
\]
is the exact affine-minor form of the tensor.

Here is a proof including its sign and scalar. After translating
the columns, write \(C_1=(C_{1ij})\), \(C_2=(C_{2ij})\),
\(v_1=(C_{11i})_i\), and \(v_2=(C_{12i})_i\).
The lower-right block of \(R^tB_t\) is formed from
the first \(m-1\) columns of \(S\), followed by \(v_t\);
its first column is \((a,0,\ldots,0)^t\).

Insert row weights \(1+\epsilon z_{i2}\) into
\(R^tB_1\), and weights \(1+\epsilon z_{i1}\)
into \(R^tB_2\), and subtract the determinant derivatives.
The two fourth-moment last columns are identical and
cancel. The extra Schur-complement columns are multiples
of column two or column one of \(S\), respectively,
so their determinants vanish by repeated columns.
The remaining derivative is exactly
\[
a\left(v_1^t(d\,\operatorname{adj}_S[C_2])e_m
       -v_2^t(d\,\operatorname{adj}_S[C_1])e_m\right)
=-aF_{a,m}.
\tag{HC.11}
\]
To verify the last equality directly at invertible \(S\),
\[
d\,\operatorname{adj}_S[M]
=\det(S)\{\operatorname{tr}(GM)G-GMG\}.
\]
Substitution is precisely minus the two cofactor sums
in (HC.8). Both sides are polynomial, so the identity
holds also at singular \(S\).

Weighted Cauchy–Binet computes the same derivative as
\[
\sum_I\det R_I
\left((\sum_{i\in I}z_{i2})\det(B_1)_I
      -(\sum_{i\in I}z_{i1})\det(B_2)_I\right).
\]
The determinants do not change on translating their
columns: the quadratic corrections use only \(1,w_1,w_2\),
which are present. Substituting \(z=w-\bar w\) and
multiplying by \(a\) gives exactly (HC.10).

The right side has degree at most three in each row.
For a row outside \(I\) the degree is at most one.
For a row in \(I\), all terms of degree four must
use its linear entry in \(R\), its quadratic entry
in \(B_t\), and its own entry in \(L_{I,p}\).
The cofactors of the last columns in \(B_1,B_2\)
are identical. The two row factors are
\(w_{i2}w_{i1}^2\) and \(w_{i1}(w_{i1}w_{i2})\);
they cancel term for term, with the same coefficient
\(a-m-1\). Every remaining term has degree at most
three. This verifies the finite extension directly.

## 4. A uniform nonzero specialization

Take centered rows
\[
e_1,\ldots,e_m,\quad v=e_1+2e_2,\quad
-u=-2e_1-3e_2-e_3-\cdots-e_m,
\quad a-m-2\text{ zeros}.
\tag{HC.12}
\]
Then \(u=\mathbf1+v\), \(S=I+vv^t+uu^t\), and
\[
\Delta=\det S=6m+8,\qquad
G=I-[v,u]
\begin{pmatrix}6&8\\8&m+12\end{pmatrix}^{-1}
[v,u]^t.
\tag{HC.13}
\]
Multiplication verifies this inverse, and the two-by-two
determinant gives \(\Delta\).
The third-moment slices and vectors are
\[
C_1=e_1e_1^t+vv^t-2uu^t,\quad
C_2=e_2e_2^t+2vv^t-3uu^t,\quad
v_1=e_1+v-4u,\quad v_2=2v-6u.
\]
For transparency, all scalar products needed in (HC.8)
reduce to the following six entries of (HC.13):

| Expression | Exact value |
|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{tr}(GC_1)\) | \((-2m-4)/\Delta\) |
| \(\operatorname{tr}(GC_2)\) | \((-6m-12)/\Delta\) |
| \((Gv_1)_m\) | \(-36/\Delta\) |
| \((Gv_2)_m\) | \(-52/\Delta\) |
| \((GC_2Gv_1)_m\) | \((336m+592)/\Delta^2\) |
| \((GC_1Gv_2)_m\) | \((344m+528)/\Delta^2\) |

The inverse formula gives every entry by ordinary matrix
multiplication. Substituting them into
\[
F_{a,m}=\Delta\bigl[
(GC_2Gv_1)_m-\operatorname{tr}(GC_2)(Gv_1)_m
-(GC_1Gv_2)_m+\operatorname{tr}(GC_1)(Gv_2)_m
\bigr]
\]
gives the numerator \(-120m-160=-20\Delta\).
Consequently
\[
F_{a,m}=-20,\qquad D_{a,m}=20a^2\ne0
\quad(a\ge m+2).
\tag{HC.14}
\]
The appended zero rows change neither \(S\) nor \(C\).

Put \(u_0=\prod_i x_i\), and define the homogeneous
highest polynomial
\[
\widehat D_{a,n,m}=u_0^nD_{a,m}(y_i/x_i).
\tag{HC.15}
\]
The degree-three cancellation in §3 proves that this
is polynomial for every \(n\ge3\). It has separate
degree \(n\), weight \(\lambda\), and is nonzero by
(HC.14). The first-coordinate raising equations are
its translation invariance, and the remaining equations
are (HC.9). Dehomogenization at \(x_i=1\) injects the
whole highest space into \((S_\nu\mathfrak h_a)^{S_a}\),
as explicitly proved in R-039 after HO.13.
Together with (HC.5), this proves the target multiplicity
one in (HC.2).

## 5. The normalized determinant derivative and canonical scalar

Let \(L\) be an independent-row formal functional
with first moments zero. Its second and third tensors
are denoted by \(U,C\). Extend it arbitrarily to degree
four for the following determinant derivatives; the
result will have no dependence on that extension.

In the expectation of (HC.10), every outside-row
weight vanishes by its first moment. For a fixed
subset \(I\), the expectation of its inside weighted
determinant difference is the difference of derivatives
of the two moment matrices. The exact two-determinant
permutation expansion contributes \((m+1)!\), as
in HO.14. The first column of the unweighted moment
matrix is \((1,0,\ldots,0)^t\).
The same Schur-complement computation as (HC.11),
now with upper-left entry one, gives
\(-(m+1)!F(U,C)\). Its fourth-moment last columns
cancel, and its remaining extra columns repeat one
of the first \(m-1\) columns of \(U\).
There are \(\binom a{m+1}\) subsets and an inside
coefficient \(a-m-1\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{
L^{\otimes a}(D_{a,m})=-(a)_{m+2}F(U,C).}
\tag{HC.16}
\]
The complete cancellation of the arbitrary fourth
moments makes this computation valid for a functional
originally defined only through degree three.

For a normalized split form of degree \(n\ge3\),
the exact centered moments HO.16 give
\[
U=-S_n/[n(n-1)],\qquad
C=2C_n/[n(n-1)(n-2)].
\]
The cofactor in (HC.7) has degree \(m-2\) in \(S\),
and (HC.8) has degree two in \(C\). Hence
\[
F(U,C)=
\frac{4(-1)^{m-2}}
{n^m(n-1)^m(n-2)^2}F_{n,m}.
\]
Using \(D_{n,m}=-n^2F_{n,m}\), the actual canonical
pairing now yields
\[
\boxed{
h_{a,n}\widehat D_{a,n,m}
=\frac{4(-1)^{m-2}(a)_{m+2}}
{n^{m+2}(n-1)^m(n-2)^2}\widehat D_{n,a,m}.}
\tag{HC.17}
\]
This identity uses the scalar-one normalized grid map
SR.5–SR.6. Homogeneity extends the evaluation with
first coordinates one to the dense nonzero first-coordinate
open set and then to the polynomial identity everywhere.
In particular, no degree-four moment of a cubic split
form has been assigned by a zero-denominator formula.

For \(a,n\ge m+2\), the scalar and both vectors are
nonzero. An explicit preimage of \(\widehat D_{a,n,m}\)
under \(h_{n,a}\) is
\[
\boxed{
\frac{(-1)^{m-2}a^{m+2}(a-1)^m(a-2)^2}
{4(n)_{m+2}}\widehat D_{n,a,m}.}
\tag{HC.18}
\]
For \(3\le n\le m\), source length gives zero, since
the source outer degree is \(n\) and \(\lambda\) has
\(m+1\) rows. At \(n=m+1\), the exact complement
map (HC.6) and the invariant exclusion following it
give source multiplicity zero. These facts prove
every zero endpoint in (HC.2). They also agree with
(HC.10): the subset sum is empty below \(m+1\),
and both its inside and outside coefficients vanish
at exactly \(m+1\).

All tensor, complementary-column, determinant, and
Young maps are rational. They therefore have the same
multiplicity matrices in every declared ambient rank.
R-036 §5 gives the precise frame-torsor, SGA/EGA,
representation-\(K_0\), and cote133/028 transport
for these maps. The Chow coordinate-ring realization
is the exact pullback R-037 EP.3–EP.5, in particular
the algebra morphism EP.4.

## 6. Executed finite checks

The script verify_four_three_one_tail_family.py
expands the actual weighted determinant products and
the split linear forms, and pairs their monomials
with exact multinomial denominators. The degree-four
row terms are canceled directly by their identical
quadratic-column factors, before evaluating any
inner-degree-three pairing. It checks two configurations
with nonunit first coordinates at \(a=5,6\),
\(3\le n\le6\), \(3\le m\le\min(a-2,4)\).
All 24 literal scalar checks pass. In every case the
weighted minor sum also equals \(-n^2\) times the
separately computed centered complementary-minor
tensor, including every zero endpoint.

The same script independently computes all 45 target
and 45 source coefficients for \(4\le a\le8\),
\(3\le n\le5\), \(3\le m\le a-1\). They agree
with the unit ranges and the \(a=m+1\) and
\(n=m+1\) zero endpoints. The receipts are
FOUR_THREE_ONE_TAIL_CANONICAL_CHECK.tsv and
FOUR_THREE_ONE_TAIL_MN_CHECK.tsv.
These finite checks supplement the complete unbounded
map and multiplicity proof above.


# A complete three-dimensional higher-row canonical block

## R-041. The tails \((4,2^{m-1})\)

Let \(m\ge2\), \(a\ge m+1\), \(n\ge4\), and \(\dim V\ge m+1\).
Define
\[
\lambda=(an-2m-2,4,2^{m-1}),\qquad
r_t=\min(3,\max(0,t-m)).
\tag{QE.1}
\]
The first part is at least \(2m+2\ge4\).
The exact target and canonical-image multiplicities are
\[
\boxed{
a_{a,n}^{\lambda}=r_a,\qquad
\operatorname{mult}_{\lambda}\operatorname{im}h_{n,a}
=\min(r_a,r_n).}
\tag{QE.2}
\]
In particular, the full three-dimensional target component is reached
for every \(a,n\ge m+3\). The proof gives its explicit three-by-three
canonical matrix and inverse, as well as all one- and two-dimensional
endpoint ranks. No historical novelty assertion is made.

## 1. Three centered highest polynomials and their row degrees

Use centered rows \(z_i=w_i-\bar w\in\mathbb Q^m\), and put
\[
S=\sum_i z_i z_i^t,\quad
C=(\sum_i z_{i1}z_{ip}z_{iq})_{pq},\quad
D=(\sum_i z_{i1}^2z_{ip}z_{iq})_{pq}.
\]
Define
\[
P_1=S_{11}\det S,\qquad
P_2=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(S)D),\qquad
P_3=[t^2]\det(S+tC).
\tag{QE.3}
\]
These are polynomials also at singular \(S\).
At invertible \(S\), with \(G=S^{-1}\), the last is
\[
P_3=\frac{\det S}{2}
\left((\operatorname{tr}(GC))^2-\operatorname{tr}(GCGC)\right).
\tag{QE.4}
\]
The determinant's second derivative, or its two-permutation expansion,
proves this formula and its factor.

All three are row-symmetric and translation invariant. They are highest
polynomials of lower weight \((4,2^{m-1})\): each has determinant-square
weight \((2^m)\), with two additional covariant indices equal to one.
For \(P_2\) these are the two uncontracted indices of the fourth tensor;
for \(P_3\) they are the two uncontracted indices of its third-tensor
slices. Adjugate congruence and the complementary-minor version of
(QE.4) give the exact tensor transformations. All raising operators
therefore kill these components.

Here are polynomial maps proving the separate degree bound.
Let \(R\) have rows \((1,w_i)\), let \(k=m+1\), and write
\(f_I=\det R_I^2\). Put \(s_i=z_{i1}\), and define
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=(\sum_i s_i^2)\sum_{|I|=k}f_I,\\
B&=\sum_{|I|=k}(\sum_{i\in I}s_i^2)f_I,\\
C'&=\sum_{|I|=k}e_2((s_i)_{i\in I})f_I.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{A=aP_1,\qquad B=P_1+aP_2,\qquad C'=aP_3-P_1.}
\tag{QE.5}
\]
For the first equality, centered Cauchy–Binet gives
\(\det(R^tR)=a\det S=\sum_I f_I\).
For the second, insert row weights \(1+t s_i^2\).
The first determinant derivative has top-left contribution
\(S_{11}\det S\), and lower-block contribution
\(a\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(S)D)\).
Weighted Cauchy–Binet gives exactly \(B\).
For the third, insert weights \(1+t s_i\). Its centered Gram matrix is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}a&t(Se_1)^t\\tSe_1&S+tC\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Schur-complement determinant, through degree two, is
\(a\det(S+tC)-t^2\det S\,S_{11}\).
Weighted Cauchy–Binet gives \(C'\) as the coefficient of \(t^2\).
This proves (QE.5), with its signs. The invertible-matrix calculation
extends polynomially to singular matrices.

Each \(f_I\) has degree at most two in each row. Each displayed weight
has degree at most two in every row, even after expanding the common
mean. Thus \(A,B,C'\), and hence all \(P_j\), have row degree at most four.

For slots \((x_i,y_i)\), let \(u=\prod_i x_i\) and
\[
\widehat P_{j;a,n,m}=u^nP_j(y_i/x_i).
\tag{QE.6}
\]
These are polynomial highest vectors of weight \(\lambda\) for
\(n\ge4\). Dehomogenization gives the literal inverse on their span
and is injective on the whole fixed-degree highest space.

## 2. The invariant bound and exact finite-row restriction

In the four-column invariant algebra HO.3, the transpose of the present
tail is \(\gamma=(m,m,1,1)\). Exterior degree zero contributes twice:
in the paired shape \((p+l,p+l,q+l,q+l)\), take
\((l,q,p)=(0,1,m)\) or \((1,0,m-1)\).
Exterior degree two uses
\(\Lambda^2(\Lambda^3T)=(\det T)\otimes\Lambda^2T\).
The fourth part one forces \(q=l=0\), and the unique vertical
two-strip adds rows one and two to \((m-1,m-1,1,1)\).
Equivalently \(p=m-2\) in the paired shape before the determinant
factor. Exterior degree four has fourth part at least three.
These exhaustive exterior/Pieri maps, with HO.5's exact Pfaffian
decomposition, prove
\[
\dim(S_{(4,2^{m-1})}\mathfrak h_a)^{S_a}\le3.
\tag{QE.7}
\]

We also need actual surjectivity when reducing the number of rows.
For \(A_0\ge a\), let
\(\iota:\mathfrak h_a\hookrightarrow\mathfrak h_{A_0}\)
pad a vector by zeros, and let \(q=\iota^t\) for the ordinary invariant
dot products. Explicitly
\[
q(P_{A_0}e_i)=
\begin{cases}P_a e_i,&i\le a,\\0,&i>a.\end{cases}
\tag{QE.8}
\]
The exterior map \(\Lambda(q\otimes1_T)\) therefore sends every row
power-sum generator in HO.3 with \(A_0\) rows to its generator with
\(a\) rows. Those generators span the entire finite-row invariant
algebra, by HO.3's signed equality-partition proof.
Thus the map sends the \(S_{A_0}\)-invariant algebra onto the
\(S_a\)-invariant algebra. It is \(GL(T)\)-equivariant.
Taking the actual skew-Cauchy Young summand of weight \(\gamma\)
gives the corresponding surjection on \(S_\nu\)-invariants.

Under the invariant dot products, its polynomial realization is
restriction to \(\iota(\mathfrak h_a)\). There the rows sum to zero,
so padding zeros changes neither \(S,C,D\). Consequently
\[
P_{j;A_0}|_{\iota(\mathfrak h_a)}=P_{j;a}\quad(j=1,2,3)
\tag{QE.9}
\]
with scalar one. This exact map will establish spanning at every
finite row count.

## 3. The exact independent-row matrix

Let \(L\) have first moments zero, with arbitrary second, third and
fourth moments. Denote its second matrix by \(U\), its first-coordinate
third slice by \(C_0\), and its twice-first-coordinate fourth slice by
\(D_0\). Write
\[
Q=U_{11}\det U,\quad
R=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(U)D_0),\quad
T=[t^2]\det(U+tC_0).
\]
For each fixed \(I\) of size \(k=m+1\), put
\(T_I=\sum_{i\in I}w_{i1}\), \(U_I=\sum_{i\in I}w_{i1}^2\),
and use \(T_{\rm all},U_{\rm all}\) for the entire row set.
Let \(l=a-k\). The following expectation table is divided by \(k!\):

| Polynomial paired with \(f_I\) | Value after division by \(k!\) |
|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(\det U\) |
| \(U_I\) | \(Q+R\) |
| \(T_I^2\) | \(R+2T-Q\) |
| \(U_{\rm all}\) | \(R+(l+1)Q\) |
| \(T_{\rm all}^2\) | \(R+2T+(l-1)Q\) |
| \(T_{\rm all}T_I\) | \(R+2T-Q\) |

The first entry is the exact two-determinant pairing HO.14.
For \(U_I\), take the first derivative of its moment matrix with row
weight \(w_1^2\); the top-left entry is \(U_{11}\), and the lower block
is \(D_0\). For \(e_2(w_I)\), take the second coefficient of its moment
matrix with weight \(w_1\). The Gram block calculation of §1, now
with top-left entry one, gives \(T-Q\).
Since \(T_I^2=U_I+2e_2(w_I)\), this proves the third entry.
The remaining entries follow by independent outside rows:
their first moments vanish and their total squared first coordinate
has expectation \(lU_{11}\). This proves the full table.

Before pairing, the weights of \(A,B,C'\) in (QE.5) are respectively
\[
\begin{aligned}
&U_{\rm all}-T_{\rm all}^2/a,\\
&U_I-2T_{\rm all}T_I/a+kT_{\rm all}^2/a^2,\\
&(T_I^2-U_I)/2-(k-1)T_{\rm all}T_I/a
 +k(k-1)T_{\rm all}^2/(2a^2).
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(\binom a{k}\) subsets, so the common factor is \((a)_k\).
Substitute the table and use (QE.5) to return to \(P_1,P_2,P_3\).
The result is
\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}L^{\otimes a}P_1\\L^{\otimes a}P_2\\L^{\otimes a}P_3\end{pmatrix}
=(a)_{m+1}\mathcal C_{a,m}
\begin{pmatrix}Q\\R\\T\end{pmatrix},}
\tag{QE.10}
\]
where
\[
\mathcal C_{a,m}=
{\setlength{\arraycolsep}{3pt}\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{a^2-am-a+m+2}{a^2}&\dfrac{a-1}{a^2}&-\dfrac2{a^2}\\[3pt]
\dfrac{(m+2)(2a-m-2)}{a^3}&\dfrac{a^2-3a+m+2}{a^3}
&-\dfrac{2(2a-m-2)}{a^3}\\[3pt]
\dfrac{(m-1)(m+2)(a-m-2)}{2a^3}
&-\dfrac{(m-1)(2a-m-2)}{2a^3}
&\dfrac{a^2-2am+m^2+m-2}{a^3}
\end{pmatrix}}.
\tag{QE.11}
\]
Direct determinant expansion gives
\[
\boxed{\det\mathcal C_{a,m}
=\frac{(a-m-2)(a-m-1)^2}{a^5}.}
\tag{QE.12}
\]
Every entry comes from the displayed finite table.
The determinant can also be checked after multiplying the rows
by \(a^2,a^3,2a^3\), respectively.

The formal polynomials \(Q,R,T\) are independent for \(m\ge2\).
Set \(U=I\). Zero third and fourth tensors give \(Q=1,R=T=0\);
varying the symmetric fourth entry \(D_{1111}\) varies \(R\)
independently. Finally take third entries \(C_{111}=C_{122}=1\),
with all other entries not forced by symmetry zero.
Its slice has two diagonal ones, so \(T=1\).
Thus (QE.12) proves independence of the actual \(P_1,P_2,P_3\)
whenever \(a\ge m+3\). With (QE.7), they form the entire invariant
basis. Equations (QE.8)–(QE.9) then prove that their finite-row
images span for every smaller row count as well.

## 4. Finite-row relations and target multiplicities

At \(a=m+1\), the sole subset \(I\) is the full row set.
In centered coordinates \(B=A\) and \(C'=-A/2\). Hence
\[
P_2=\frac{a-1}{a}P_1,\qquad
P_3=\frac{2-a}{2a}P_1.
\tag{QE.13}
\]
The centered simplex \(e_1,\ldots,e_m,-\mathbf1\) has
\(P_1=2(m+1)\ne0\). The invariant dimension is one.

At \(a=m+2\), write \(I=[a]\setminus\{i\}\).
The centered identities \(T_I=-w_{i1}\) and
\(U_I=U_{\rm all}-w_{i1}^2\) give \(B+C'=A/2\). Thus
\[
P_2+P_3=P_1/2.
\tag{QE.14}
\]
The minor in rows one and two, columns one and two of
\(\mathcal C_{m+2,m}\) equals \((m-1)/(m+2)^3\ne0\).
The independence argument of §3 shows that \(P_1,P_2\) are
independent, so the invariant dimension is two.

For \(a\le m\), every subset sum in (QE.5) is empty.
All \(P_j\) vanish, and their proved spanning gives invariant
dimension zero. With §3, the dimension at every positive row count
is exactly \(r_a\).

For \(n\ge4\), every \(P_j\) extends by (QE.6).
Dehomogenization injects the highest multiplicity space into this
invariant space, with inverse (QE.6) on its spanning generators.
The target multiplicity is therefore exactly \(r_a\), proving
the first assertion of (QE.2).

## 5. The actual normalized canonical matrix

Let \(N_2=n(n-1)\), \(N_3=n(n-1)(n-2)\),
\(N_4=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\).
For centered split factors, the normalized moments are
\[
U=-S_n/N_2,\qquad C_0=2C_n/N_3,
\]
and
\[
(D_0)_{ij}=
\{(S_n)_{11}(S_n)_{ij}
+2(S_n)_{1i}(S_n)_{1j}-6(D_n)_{ij}\}/N_4.
\tag{QE.15}
\]
The fourth numerator is the inclusion–exclusion sum over the three
two-pair partitions and the six four-equal permutations; singleton
blocks vanish by centering. This includes repeated coordinate labels
with their exact ordered-index factors.

It follows that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}Q\\R\\T\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{N_2^{m+1}}\mathcal D_{n,m}
\begin{pmatrix}P_{1;n}\\P_{2;n}\\P_{3;n}\end{pmatrix},
\tag{QE.16}
\]
where
\[
\mathcal D_{n,m}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0\\
(m+2)u_n&-6u_n&0\\
0&0&-4v_n
\end{pmatrix},\quad
u_n=\frac{n(n-1)}{(n-2)(n-3)},\quad
v_n=\frac{n(n-1)}{(n-2)^2}.
\tag{QE.17}
\]
The middle row uses
\(\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}S\,S)=m\det S\) and
\((Se_1)^t\operatorname{adj}S(Se_1)=S_{11}\det S\).
The last uses degree \(m-2\) in \(S\) and degree two in the third
slice in (QE.4). Thus all signs and denominators are fixed.

Combining (QE.10) and (QE.16) proves the normalized canonical identity
\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
h_{a,n}\widehat P_{1;a,n,m}\\
h_{a,n}\widehat P_{2;a,n,m}\\
h_{a,n}\widehat P_{3;a,n,m}
\end{pmatrix}
=c_{a,n,m}\mathcal C_{a,m}\mathcal D_{n,m}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat P_{1;n,a,m}\\
\widehat P_{2;n,a,m}\\
\widehat P_{3;n,a,m}
\end{pmatrix},\quad
c_{a,n,m}=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}(a)_{m+1}}{N_2^{m+1}}.}
\tag{QE.18}
\]
This display uses rows for images of source generators.
The ordinary column-coordinate matrix is its transpose.

When \(a=3\), the individual expressions on the right can be rational
homogeneous functions; their displayed linear combinations are
precisely the actual polynomial images on the left.
The identity is first the dehomogenized pairing, so this endpoint
introduces no unproved extension. For \(a\ge4\), all entries
on both sides are polynomial by (QE.6).
The exact split-form evaluation is SR.5–SR.6 with the same
normalization. First-coordinate scaling gives the identity on the
dense nonzero open set, and polynomial equality extends it everywhere.

## 6. Full rank and every finite endpoint

For \(a,n\ge m+3\), both bases have size three.
The matrix determinant is nonzero because
\(\det\mathcal D_{n,m}=24u_nv_n\ne0\) and (QE.12) is nonzero.
In column coordinates the matrix is
\[
\mathcal M_{a,n,m}
=c_{a,n,m}(\mathcal C_{a,m}\mathcal D_{n,m})^t.
\tag{QE.19}
\]
An actual preimage under \(h_{n,a}\) of a target coordinate column
\(v\) is the source combination with coordinate column
\(\mathcal M_{n,a,m}^{-1}v\), where
\[
\mathcal M_{n,a,m}^{-1}
=c_{n,a,m}^{-1}
(\mathcal C_{n,m}^{-1})^t(\mathcal D_{a,m}^{-1})^t.
\tag{QE.20}
\]
The inverses can equivalently be read as adjugate over the explicit
determinants. This gives every preimage by a fixed rational
three-by-three formula.

For endpoints, retain the first generator as basis at row count
\(m+1\), and the first two at row count \(m+2\), using
(QE.13)–(QE.14). At row counts at least \(m+3\), use all three.
For \(n\le m\), the right side of (QE.18) vanishes.
When exactly one of \(a,n\) is at least \(m+3\), the invertible
factor in that parameter and the finite-row independent basis give
rank equal to the smaller dimension. The remaining blocks have
the following literal reductions of
\(\mathcal C_{a,m}\mathcal D_{n,m}\); the nonzero common scalar
\(c_{a,n,m}\) is omitted:

| Parameters | Exact nonzero coefficient or determinant |
|---|---|
| \(a=n=m+1,\ m\ge3\) | \((m-2)/(m-1)\) |
| \(a=n=m+2\) | \(-2(m+1)(3m+2)/(m^3(m+2))\) |
| \(a=m+1,\ n=m+2\) | coefficient of the second target basis vector is \(-2(m+2)^2(3m-2)/(m^2(m-1)(m+1))\) |

The second entry is the two-by-two determinant after replacing
\(P_3\) by \(P_1/2-P_2\). The first replaces \(P_2,P_3\)
using (QE.13). The third replaces only the target \(P_3\)
using (QE.14). Substitution in (QE.11) and (QE.17) gives every
printed fraction. Reverse the off-diagonal pair by the exact
scalar-one transposition of canonical maps SR.5.
The square \(m=2,a=n=3\) lies outside \(n\ge4\).

For precision, when the larger row count occurs on the target side
of (QE.18), its three generators are independent, and the indicated
one or two rows of \(\mathcal C\) have full rank.
When it occurs on the source side, \(\mathcal C\mathcal D\) is
invertible and maps onto the span of the finite target generators.
This proves the mixed-size assertion by the actual matrix.
Thus \(h_{a,n}\) has rank \(\min(r_a,r_n)\); scalar-one
transposition gives (QE.2).

All identifications are rational tensor, column, Young, determinant
and affine-chart maps. Their multiplicity matrices are the same in
every dimension at least \(m+1\). Their Chow pullback is
R-037 EP.3–EP.5; frame-torsor and representation-\(K_0\) transport
uses the SGA/EGA/cote locators in R-036 §5.

## 7. Executed checks

The script verify_four_even_tail_block.py expands the determinant
squares, their raw row weights, and the actual split form.
It sums literal monomial pairings with exact multinomial
denominators and compares all three generators with (QE.18).
It does not call the moment table on the literal side.
Population configurations are selected to give the full separately
computed generator rank \(r_n\); nonunit first coordinates are retained.

Its ranges are \(m=2,3\), \(n=4,5,6\), together with
\((m,n)=(4,5),(4,6),(4,7)\), and \(m+1\le a\le7\).
All 246 literal generator pairings pass, including every one- and
two-dimensional endpoint and several three-dimensional matrices.

An independent cycle-index/Murnaghan–Nakayama calculation checks
the target multiplicities for \(3\le a\le8\), \(n=4,5\),
\(2\le m\le a-1\).
The receipts are `FOUR_EVEN_TAIL_CANONICAL_MATRIX_CHECK.tsv` and
`FOUR_EVEN_TAIL_MN_CHECK.tsv`.
The unbounded rank law follows from the complete matrix proof.



# The remaining inner degrees of the higher-row width-four block

## R-042. Exact cubic extension, canonical scalar, and quadratic endpoint

Let \(m\ge2\), \(a\ge m+1\), \(\dim V\ge m+1\), and
\[
\lambda=(3a-2m-2,4,2^{m-1}).
\]
Require \(\lambda_1\ge4\); among these parameters this excludes
only \((a,m)=(3,2)\). Then
\[
\boxed{
a_{a,3}^{\lambda}=\min(2,\max(0,a-m-1)),\qquad
\operatorname{mult}_{\lambda}\operatorname{im}h_{3,a}
=\begin{cases}1,&m=2,\\0,&m\ge3.\end{cases}}
\tag{QD.1}
\]
The proof specifies the whole polynomial-extension subspace and
the exact nonzero scalar in the three-row case. Together with
R-041, this determines the actual rank for every inner degree
at least three on the same tail family.

For the quadratic inner degree, the valid partitions of this form
have \(a\ge m+3\). They satisfy
\[
\boxed{
a_{a,2}^{(2a-2m-2,4,2^{m-1})}=1,\qquad
\operatorname{mult}_{(2a-2m-2,4,2^{m-1})}\operatorname{im}h_{2,a}=0.}
\tag{QD.2}
\]
The quadratic statement is the explicit principal-minor realization
of the established even-partition decomposition; its maps and
uniqueness are proved in §4. No historical novelty claim is made.

## 1. The exact degree-four row coefficient

Use R-041's three centered polynomials \(P_1,P_2,P_3\).
They span the entire relevant invariant space, of dimension
\(r_a=\min(3,a-m)\), by its explicit invariant restriction map.
Every polynomial has row degree at most four.
Write
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_1&=(a-1)/a^2,\\
\beta_2&=(a^2-3a+m+2)/a^3,\\
\beta_3&=-(m-1)(2a-m-2)/(2a^3).
\end{aligned}
\tag{QD.3}
\]
These are the second column of the exact matrix \(\mathcal C_{a,m}\).

For a fixed row \(r\), replace \(w_r\) by \(tv\) and take
the coefficient of \(t^4\). The three coefficients are exactly
\[
[t^4]P_j(w_1,\ldots,tv,\ldots,w_a)
=\beta_j\,W_r(v;w_{i\ne r}),
\tag{QD.4}
\]
where
\[
W_r=v_1^2\sum_{\substack{|I|=m+1\\r\in I}}
\left([t]\det R_I(w_r=tv)\right)^2.
\]
Here \(R\) is the affine row matrix \((1,w_i)\) of R-041.

To verify (QD.4), use the raw row weights before QE.10.
For \(I\ni r\), the leading quadratic coefficients of the
weights of \(A,B,C'\) are, respectively,
\[
\frac{a-1}{a}v_1^2,\qquad
\left(1-\frac2a+\frac{m+1}{a^2}\right)v_1^2,\qquad
\left(-\frac m a+\frac{m(m+1)}{2a^2}\right)v_1^2.
\]
The determinant square contributes its leading quadratic coefficient.
For \(I\not\ni r\), its determinant is independent of \(w_r\),
so its total row degree is at most two and cannot contribute.
Return to \(P_1,P_2,P_3\) by QE.5:
\(P_1=A/a\), \(P_2=(B-P_1)/a\), \(P_3=(C'+P_1)/a\).
The resulting three factors are exactly (QD.3).

The common polynomial \(W_r\) is nonzero. Take \(v=e_1\),
and among the other rows use \(0,e_2,\ldots,e_m\);
there are enough rows because \(a\ge m+1\).
The determinant of that affine subset has nonzero linear coefficient
in \(t\). On real inputs all summands in \(W_r\) are squares,
so their sum is positive for this specialization.
Thus (QD.4) gives a nonzero linear functional on the actual
invariant span. Any linear relation among the \(P_j\)'s also
annihilates \(\beta\), by (QD.4), so it is well defined on that span.

## 2. The full cubic extension and its actual basis

A separately homogeneous polynomial of slot degree three
dehomogenizes to a polynomial of degree at most three in every
row. Conversely, multiplying such a dehomogenization by
\((\prod_i x_i)^3\) is its exact polynomial homogenization.
Since the present row degrees are at most four, (QD.4) proves
that the extension space is precisely the kernel of \(\beta\).

Because \(\beta_1\ne0\), that kernel is spanned by
\[
Q_2=\beta_1P_2-\beta_2P_1,\qquad
Q_3=\beta_1P_3-\beta_3P_1.
\tag{QD.5}
\]
Each has degree at most three in every row, by the literal
degree-four cancellation in (QD.4).
For \(a\ge m+3\), the \(P_j\)'s are independent, so
\(Q_2,Q_3\) are independent.
For \(a=m+2\), QE.14 gives \(Q_3=-Q_2\), with
\(Q_2\ne0\) because \(P_1,P_2\) are independent.
For \(a=m+1\), QE.13 gives both \(Q_j=0\).
The kernel dimension is therefore \(r_a-1\), exactly the
target multiplicity in (QD.1).

The actual highest polynomials are
\[
\widehat Q_{j;a,3,m}
=\left(\prod_i x_i\right)^3Q_j(y_i/x_i).
\tag{QD.6}
\]
Translation invariance and the lower highest-weight equations
are inherited from \(P_j\); separate homogeneity proves injectivity
of the inverse evaluation \(x_i=1\).
This identifies the entire finite-degree multiplicity space,
including its one-dimensional and zero-dimensional endpoints.

## 3. The exact cubic canonical maps

For \(m=2\), the independent-row coefficient rows in QE.10,
after applying the combinations (QD.5), are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
&Q&R&T\\ \hline
Q_2&-(a-3)^2/a^3&0&-2(a-3)/a^4\\
Q_3&(a-3)/a^3&0&(a-3)(a-2)/a^4.
\end{array}
\tag{QD.7}
\]
The common factor is \((a)_3=a(a-1)(a-2)\).
These entries are direct substitution into QE.11.
Their zero middle column agrees with the pointwise extension proof;
it removes all dependence on fourth moments before the split-form
evaluation is taken.

For three centered split factors in dimension two, the second and
third moments are \(-S_3/6\) and \(C_3/3\).
The exact three-row relations QE.13 give
\(P_{3;3}=-P_{1;3}/6\).
Consequently the formal quantities in (QD.7) are
\[
Q=-P_{1;3}/216,\qquad T=-P_{1;3}/54.
\tag{QD.8}
\]
No fourth moment is needed. One may extend the degree-three row
functional arbitrarily to degree four when deriving QE.10:
the middle column in (QD.7) cancels that extension identically.

The normalized canonical identities are therefore
\[
\boxed{
h_{a,3}\widehat Q_{2;a,3,2}
=\frac{(a-3)(a-2)(a-1)(a^2-3a+8)}
{216a^3}\widehat P_{1;3,a,2},}
\tag{QD.9}
\]
and
\[
h_{a,3}\widehat Q_{3;a,3,2}
=-\frac{(a-3)(a-2)(a-1)(5a-8)}
{216a^3}\widehat P_{1;3,a,2}.
\tag{QD.10}
\]
Their derivation is the actual scalar-one split-form pairing
SR.5–SR.6, followed by dense first-coordinate extension.
The target generator is nonzero by the centered simplex.
For every \(a\ge4\), the coefficient in (QD.9) is nonzero:
all linear factors are positive and \(a^2-3a+8>0\).
The target of this multiplicity map is the whole line
\((S_{(4,2)}\mathfrak h_3)^{S_3}\), whose dimension is one
by R-041. Thus this actual map has rank one.
Its scalar reciprocal gives an explicit preimage of that
line, and scalar-one transposition gives rank one for \(h_{3,a}\).

For \(m\ge3\), the partition has \(m+1\ge4\) rows.
The source of \(h_{3,a}\) is a submodule of
\((\operatorname{Sym}^aV)^{\otimes3}\).
The three horizontal-strip Pieri inclusions have at most
three rows, so its \(\lambda\)-multiplicity is zero.
This proves the remaining actual zero ranks in (QD.1).
It is also visible in the moment map: the three-row covariance
and third tensors have a common row span of dimension at most two,
so all \(P_j\) of \(m\)-dimensional determinant type vanish.

## 4. The quadratic endpoint by actual symmetric-matrix maps

Let \(r=m+1\) and let \(Z\) be a generic symmetric \(r\)-by-\(r\)
matrix. Its entry \(Z_{ij}\) is evaluation on the normalized
symmetric tensor \(e_i\odot e_j\); a pure square therefore
has matrix entries \(v_i v_j\), including the off-diagonal
entries with this convention. Write \(\Delta_i\) for its leading principal minor.
For \(a\ge m+3\), the polynomial
\[
\Delta_1^{\,a-m-3}\Delta_2\Delta_{m+1}
\tag{QD.11}
\]
has degree \(a\) in the symmetric-matrix entries and weight
\((2a-2m-2,4,2^{m-1})\).
It is a nonzero highest vector in
\(\operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^2V)\).
Indeed lower unitriangular congruence preserves every leading
principal minor; these are precisely the raising invariances
in the coordinate convention used above. Diagonal congruence
gives their weights \((2^i)\).

The uniqueness can be checked by an actual dense chart.
On the open set where all \(\Delta_i\ne0\), Gaussian elimination
gives the unique factorization \(Z=L\operatorname{diag}(d_i)L^t\),
where \(L\) is lower unitriangular and
\(d_i=\Delta_i/\Delta_{i-1}\), with \(\Delta_0=1\).
These formulas and elementary elimination construct both rational
maps and their inverses on the open set.
A highest polynomial is constant on the unitriangular factor;
its fixed diagonal weight forces its restriction to be a scalar
multiple of
\(\prod_i d_i^{\lambda_i/2}\).
For the stated weight this is exactly (QD.11).
A polynomial vanishing on this dense open set is zero.
Hence its highest multiplicity is exactly one.

For the explicit slot dictionary, polarize a degree-\(a\)
matrix polynomial \(F\) by
\[
(v_1,\ldots,v_a)\longmapsto
\frac1{a!}[t_1\cdots t_a]\,
F\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^a t_i v_i v_i^t\right).
\tag{QD.12}
\]
This is symmetric and quadratic in each vector slot.
It is the normalized outer polarization followed by evaluation
on pure squares. Pure squares span the symmetric matrices;
multilinearity therefore makes this restriction injective.
The construction is the actual Cauchy/Young inclusion of the
symmetric-matrix module in the separate-slot model.
It proves the stated multiplicity in that model as well.

Finally, \(\operatorname{Sym}^2\operatorname{Sym}^aV\)
is contained in the twofold tensor product of the row-\(a\)
representation. Pieri gives at most two rows, whereas the
partition in (QD.2) has \(m+1\ge3\) rows.
Its source multiplicity is zero, and its target multiplicity
one was just proved. This proves (QD.2).

The rational homogenization, polarization, column and Gram maps
have the same fixed multiplicity maps in all declared ranks.
Their coordinate pullback is R-037 EP.3–EP.5, and their
frame-torsor and representation-\(K_0\) transport uses the
primary SGA/EGA/cote locators in R-036 §5.

## 5. Executed checks

The script verify_four_even_tail_degree_three.py expands
the determinant-square row pairings directly. It uses two
different arbitrary fourth-moment extensions of each actual
degree-three split form. The two \(Q_j\) evaluations agree
between those extensions and equal (QD.9)–(QD.10), with zero
higher-row images. Nonunit first coordinates are retained.

Its ranges are \(m=2,3,4\), \(\max(4,m+1)\le a\le8\),
with two independent configurations and both \(Q_j\)'s.
All 56 literal generator pairings and both arbitrary-extension
comparisons pass. The receipt is FOUR_EVEN_TAIL_CUBIC_SCALAR_CHECK.tsv.
It separately computes target and source plethysms by literal
cycle-index expansion and Murnaghan–Nakayama for
\(4\le a\le9\), \(2\le m\le a-1\).
All 27 target and 27 source coefficients agree.
The second receipt is FOUR_EVEN_TAIL_CUBIC_MN_CHECK.tsv.
The polynomial coefficient argument and exact scalar above
prove the unbounded extension and rank laws.



# The remaining mixed width-four block

## R-043. The tails \((4,3,2^{m-2})\)

Let \(m\ge2\), \(a\ge m+2\), \(n\ge4\), and \(\dim V\ge m+1\).
Set
\[
\lambda=(an-2m-3,4,3,2^{m-2}),\qquad
s_t=\min(2,\max(0,t-m-1)).
\tag{ME.1}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
a_{a,n}^{\lambda}=s_a,\qquad
\operatorname{mult}_{\lambda}\operatorname{im}h_{n,a}
=\min(s_a,s_n).}
\tag{ME.2}
\]
For inner degree three, the valid partitions in the same tail family
have target multiplicity one for \(a\ge m+3\), zero for
\(a\le m+2\), and canonical-image multiplicity zero throughout.
For inner degree two the target multiplicity is zero.
The proof gives the actual two-by-two matrix, its inverse, the finite
unit endpoint, and the exact cubic extension vector. No historical
novelty assertion is made.

## 1. The two highest tensors and the invariant bound

For centered rows \(z_i=w_i-\bar w\in\mathbb Q^m\), put
\[
S=\sum_i z_i z_i^t,\quad
(C_p)_{ij}=\sum_lz_{lp}z_{li}z_{lj},\quad
(D_{pq})_{ij}=\sum_lz_{lp}z_{lq}z_{li}z_{lj},
\quad f_p=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(S)C_p).
\]
Define the symmetric bilinear polynomial
\[
\mathcal B_S(X,Y)=[uv]\det(S+uX+vY).
\]
For invertible \(S\), \(G=S^{-1}\), it equals
\[
\mathcal B_S(X,Y)=\det(S)
\left(\operatorname{tr}(GX)\operatorname{tr}(GY)
-\operatorname{tr}(GXGY)\right).
\tag{ME.3}
\]
Coefficient extraction defines it at singular \(S\), and the
determinant derivative proves (ME.3).
The required polynomials are
\[
\Phi_1=S_{11}f_2-S_{12}f_1,\qquad
\Phi_2=\mathcal B_S(D_{11},C_2)-\mathcal B_S(D_{12},C_1).
\tag{ME.4}
\]
Both are symmetric in the rows and translation invariant.
Their tensor transformation is determinant-square times a
three-covariant-index hook. The two terms have free labels
\(1,1,2\), with the first two labels in their symmetric pair.
The raising operator \(E_{12}\) sends each of their two terms
to the same component with labels \(1,1,1\), so their difference
vanishes. All other raising operators kill the components.
Their diagonal weight is exactly \((4,3,2^{m-2})\).
Adjugate congruence and the complementary-minor form of (ME.3)
prove these transformation assertions as polynomial identities.

The tail transpose is \(\gamma=(m,m,2,1)\).
In HO.3's exact four-column invariant-algebra surjection,
only odd exterior degrees of \(\Lambda(\Lambda^3T)\) occur.
Exterior degree three has a determinant-square factor and hence
fourth part at least two; it misses \(\gamma\).
Exterior degree one contributes exactly twice. Using the
paired-shape decomposition HO.5, its vertical three-strip
comes from \((m-1,m-1,1,1)\) with no \(\Lambda^4T\) factor,
or from \((m-2,m-2,0,0)\) with one determinant factor.
In each case the added rows are one, two and three.
All other choices are excluded by the equal first two parts
and the final parts \(2,1\). The actual exterior Pieri projections
have multiplicity one. Consequently
\[
\dim(S_{(4,3,2^{m-2})}\mathfrak h_a)^{S_a}\le2.
\tag{ME.5}
\]

## 2. Affine Gram maps and row degree at most four

Let \(k=m+1\), let \(R\) have rows \((1,w_i)\), and write
\(f_I=\det R_I^2\). For a subset \(I\), define centered sums
\(T_{I,p}=\sum_{i\in I}z_{ip}\) and
\(U_{I,pq}=\sum_{i\in I}z_{ip}z_{iq}\).
The cubic-minor identity CT.9, in centered coordinates, gives
\[
a f_p=\sum_{|I|=k}T_{I,p}f_I.
\tag{ME.6}
\]
Its weighted-Cauchy–Binet proof applies to every component \(p\).
Thus
\[
a\Phi_1=\sum_I(S_{11}T_{I,2}-S_{12}T_{I,1})f_I.
\tag{ME.7}
\]
There is a second exact polynomial identity:
\[
\boxed{
\sum_I(U_{I,11}T_{I,2}-U_{I,12}T_{I,1})f_I
=a\Phi_2+\Phi_1.}
\tag{ME.8}
\]

To prove (ME.8), insert row weights \(1+u z_{i1}^2+v z_{i2}\)
in \(R^tR\), and subtract the mixed determinant coefficient
for weights \(1+u z_{i1}z_{i2}+v z_{i1}\).
The same-row product cancels identically, so weighted
Cauchy–Binet gives exactly the left side.
The centered base matrix is \(\operatorname{diag}(a,S)\).
Its mixed coefficient is \(a\Phi_2+\Phi_1\):
the lower-block mixed coefficient is \(a\Phi_2\);
the top-left quadratic variation gives
\(S_{11}f_2-S_{12}f_1\);
and the two off-diagonal Schur-complement contributions
are both \(-2\det(S)C_{112}\), so they cancel in the difference.
These statements also follow by multiplying the two-by-two
block inverse in the determinant's mixed derivative.
This proves the identity, including its coefficient one.

Both weight polynomials in (ME.7) and (ME.8) have degree
at most two in each fixed original row.
Indeed, under \(w_r\mapsto tv\), every centered row has
leading term \(\alpha_i tv\). The leading degree-three
term in either weight is a scalar times
\(v_1^2v_2-v_1v_2v_1=0\).
As \(f_I\) has degree at most two in each row, (ME.7)–(ME.8)
prove that \(\Phi_1,\Phi_2\) have row degree at most four.
Their separate homogenizations
\[
\widehat\Phi_{j;a,n,m}
=\left(\prod_i x_i\right)^n\Phi_j(y_i/x_i)
\tag{ME.9}
\]
are therefore polynomial highest vectors for \(n\ge4\).

## 3. The complete independent-row matrix

Let a formal row functional have first moments zero.
Use \(U,C_p^0,D_{pq}^0\) for its second, third and fourth
moments, and let \(F_1,F_2\) be the expressions (ME.4)
in these moments. Set \(l=a-k\).
Then the exact independent-row identity is
\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}L^{\otimes a}\Phi_1\\L^{\otimes a}\Phi_2\end{pmatrix}
=(a)_k\,\mathcal E_{a,m}
\begin{pmatrix}F_1\\F_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathcal E_{a,m}=
\begin{pmatrix}
l^2/a^2&l/a^2\\
kl/a^3&(a-1)l/a^3
\end{pmatrix}.}
\tag{ME.10}
\]
Here is a derivation by literal raw row sums, including all
centering terms.

For a fixed subset \(I\), use uncentered \(T_p=\sum_{i\in I}w_{ip}\),
\(U_{pq}^I=\sum_{i\in I}w_{ip}w_{iq}\),
\(W_p=\sum_iw_{ip}\), and \(U_{pq}^{\rm all}=\sum_iw_{ip}w_{iq}\).
Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
X&=U_{11}^{\rm all}T_2-U_{12}^{\rm all}T_1,\\
Y&=U_{11}^{\rm all}W_2-U_{12}^{\rm all}W_1,\\
Z&=W_1^2T_2-W_1W_2T_1.
\end{aligned}
\]
After expanding the centering in (ME.7), its contribution to
\(a^2\Phi_1\) is \((aX-kY-Z)f_I\).
Divide all expectations in the following equations by \(k!\):
\[
L(Xf_I)=F_2+(l+1)F_1,\quad
L(Yf_I)=F_2+(l+1)F_1,\quad
L(Zf_I)=lF_1.
\tag{ME.11}
\]
For the inside part of \(X\), the mixed moment-matrix derivative
in §2, now with top-left entry one, gives \(F_2+F_1\).
Its outside quadratic terms give \(lF_1\).
The additional outside first moments in \(Y-X\) vanish;
its same-row cubic difference vanishes identically.
In \(Z\), the completely inside terms cancel, the outside
linear terms have zero expectation, and the two outside
second moments leave \(lF_1\). These are all equality patterns.

For (ME.8), the centered inside weight expands exactly to
\[
J-\frac{k}{a}(W_2U_{11}^I-W_1U_{12}^I)
-\frac1a(W_1T_1T_2-W_2T_1^2),\quad
J=U_{11}^I T_2-U_{12}^I T_1.
\tag{ME.12}
\]
The expectations of the first two displayed raw differences
are both \(k!(F_1+F_2)\); the last has expectation zero.
Hence its expectation is \(k!l(F_1+F_2)/a\).
Combine this with (ME.11), the \(\binom a{k}\) subsets,
and (ME.8) to obtain every entry of (ME.10).

The determinant is
\[
\boxed{\det\mathcal E_{a,m}=l^2(l-1)/a^4.}
\tag{ME.13}
\]
Indeed its remaining numerator is
\(l(a-1)-k=a(l-1)\).
The formal \(F_1,F_2\) are independent for \(m\ge2\):
take \(U=I\) and only the third tensor \(C_{222}=1\).
Then \(F_1=1\); varying the symmetric fourth entry
\(D_{1111}\) varies \(F_2\) independently.
Thus (ME.13) proves independence of \(\Phi_1,\Phi_2\)
at every \(a\ge m+3\). With (ME.5), they form the entire
invariant basis.

The zero-padding/orthogonal-projection maps QE.8–QE.9
apply to these centered moment tensors as well:
restriction of zero-padded centered rows changes none of
\(S,C_p,D_{pq}\), so it sends each \(\Phi_j\) to the same
finite-row polynomial with scalar one.
The invariant-algebra surjection therefore proves that
their finite-row images span every smaller invariant space.
